articles.title: How I Built This and Why It Nearly Killed Me
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: The developer who locked me out, the husband with excellent timing, and six months of 5am starts.
articles.body: My husband has excellent timing. The night before we were ready to launch, he walked into the room and said: you know how you've always wanted the shop to live inside the website? Well, we can do it now. He was not wrong. It was everything I'd wanted. The shop sitting inside Beauticate, a destination woven into the same editorial world I'd spent twelve years building. One ecosystem. One experience. Content and commerce finally in the same place. It would also mean rebuilding the entire site from scratch. Twelve years of content. Seventeen hundred articles. Thousands of images. I said yes. How could I not? If I'd known what was coming, maybe I would have thought about it a little longer. What followed was six weeks that I will never forget. Waking most mornings at 5am (weekends included), working until my eyes were burning, stumbling into bed and starting again before dawn. The migration scrambled more articles than I could count. Broken images. Floating URLs. Garbled text. Articles in entirely the wrong place, looking nothing like they should. On top of onboarding all the brands for the shop, getting their listings right and building a new site from scratch, I was fixing over 1,700 articles. Some days it felt like bailing out a boat with a teaspoon. But I need to back up. Because this story actually starts about a year earlier, with a coffee. The coffee that started it I had coffee with Nicole Gazal O'Neil (of Real Housewives fame), the fabulous founder of Bonwellness — who would go on to become the very first brand to come on board for the shop, and is now stocked here. We were talking about e-comm, as you do. I was telling her how shopping guides we create are some of our most-read content. We launched our Top 100 Products list back in 2018, and I watched it drive thousands of clicks to external brand websites, losing my readers in the process. Then we did the Top 50 Skincare Products and the Sacred 60. They were beautiful to look at and useful to read, but we needed to make them more shoppable. Our Sacred Six edits on Instagram would sell products out. The Beautiful Inside podcast would convert listeners into customers for the founders we'd featured. But there was nowhere for any of that to land that was ours. Nicole asked why I hadn't built a shop. I gave her the usual answer: too complicated, too much stock, too much risk. She asked me if I'd looked at Modern Dropship. I went home and looked it up that evening. The technology had finally caught up with what I'd wanted to do for years. I could curate the products I believed in and the brands would ship directly from their own warehouses. No stock. No fulfillment headaches. The editorial model I'd always imagined, finally technically possible. That was almost a year ago. Sell the dream before you lose your nerve So I set about contacting the brands I wanted to feature, did 6 months of daily meetings, selling the dream before I even built the product. I knew I could curate the best of the best and tell stories that would sell them. I've been doing this more than half of my life. My first beauty writing gig was at an indie magazine called Your Destiny when I was 18. From there, TV Week , where I had my own beauty and fashion page (and where I once had to rub bronzing cream on Chris Hemsworth's chest during a cover shoot because the…

articles.title: The LA Effect: What Beverly Hills Taught Our Style Editor About Dressing
articles.author: Kate Waterhouse
articles.excerpt: Beauticate style editor Kate Waterhouse recently touched down in Los Angeles for a whirlwind trip that turned into something of a masterclass in effortless dressing. Here, she shares the style and wellness lessons she brought home.
articles.body: Beauticate style editor Kate Waterhouse recently touched down in Los Angeles for a whirlwind trip that turned into something of a masterclass in effortless dressing. Here, she shares the style and wellness lessons she brought home — and exactly how to steal the look. There's something about Beverly Hills that makes you recalibrate. Not because the women there are dripping in obvious luxury — quite the opposite. "One of the things that struck me most about Beverly Hills was how effortless everyone looked," says Kate. "The style is undeniably luxurious, but it's never overly polished or trying too hard. Women seem to invest in beautiful pieces that work hard in their wardrobe rather than chasing every trend." As someone who has spent years writing about fashion, Kate admitted she expected to be impressed. What she didn't expect was to feel inspired to edit her own wardrobe the moment she got home. Here's what she learned. Lunch at the iconic Beverly Hills Hotel — where the dress code is effortless and the garden terrace is as beautiful as ever. Lesson 1: Neutrals are not boring — they're a power move "I noticed a lot of neutral palettes — ivory, camel, chocolate brown, navy and black — with an emphasis on beautiful fabrics and tailoring," says Kate. "Relaxed suiting, oversized blazers, wide-leg trousers and elevated basics were everywhere. Even activewear felt polished, often paired with designer handbags, statement sunglasses and beautiful jewellery." The style is undeniably luxurious, but it's never overly polished or trying too hard. Nothing felt safe or dull, though. The women wearing these tones understood that neutrals only work when the fabric and the fit are doing the heavy lifting. Think wide-leg trousers in a beautiful drape, a perfectly cut blazer in camel, a satin slip that catches the light. The colour is the constant. The quality is what makes it sing. How to wear it now: Build your winter wardrobe around one or two tones and invest in the best fabric you can afford. Chocolate brown is having a serious moment this season — a rich, deep hue that feels luxurious without demanding attention. (The Beauticate team's winter edit is full of ways to wear it.) Outside The Beverly Hills Hotel — the pink walls never disappoint. Lesson 2: Accessories do the talking so your outfit doesn't have to If there was one consistent thread running through every great look Kate saw in Beverly Hills, it was this: one brilliant accessory worn with intention. A sculptural gold earring. A slim gold necklace sitting perfectly at the collarbone. A great pair of sunglasses that gives a look a personality of its own. "What surprised me most was how understated luxury felt," she says. "The focus wasn't on obvious logos or trend-driven dressing, but on quality, fit and confidence. There was also a real appreciation for mixing high and low pieces. A simple white T-shirt and jeans might be paired with a beautiful handbag or a perfectly cut blazer." The sunglasses, in particular, were everywhere — and not the quiet, forgettable kind. Cat-eye frames, retro-tinted lenses, architectural shapes in tortoiseshell and burgundy. The punctuation mark on an otherwise understated outfit. How to wear it now: Don't try to wear everything at once. Choose your statement piece — earrings, a necklace or sunglasses — and let the rest of the look breathe. A pair of sculptural gold earrings will transform even the most basic outfit. (For more on Kate's accessory philosophy, see her quick smoky eye tutorial — proof that one bold move is all you need.) One oversized blazer over…

articles.title: Is Sanur Bali's Best-Kept Secret? And Where to Stay
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: After three days in the chaos of Canggu, Sigourney found herself somewhere else entirely. This is her Sanur Bali hotel review — two nights at Bali Beach Hotel and The Meru Sanur, two of the most compelling places to stay in Bali right now.
articles.body: Sigourney recently travelled to Bali with her family, and after three days in the chaos of Canggu, found herself somewhere else entirely. This is her Sanur Bali hotel review: two nights at Bali Beach Hotel, The Heritage Collection, and The Meru Sanur, two of the most compelling places to stay in Bali right now. It is not the Bali you think you know. Sanur is the quieter, more culturally intact alternative to Canggu and Seminyak — and it has quietly become one of the most sophisticated destinations in Bali, anchored by two extraordinary hotels: the heritage grandeur of Bali Beach Hotel, The Heritage Collection, and the dramatic new luxury of The Meru Sanur. If you want beauty, ease and genuine culture without the noise, this is where you go. It seems that everyone goes to Canggu or Uluwatu and I get it — they're energetic and full of extraordinary food and great shopping. We did our first three days in Pererenan (next door to Canggu) with all the scooters, construction noise and beautiful chaos. By day three I was ready for a slower pace. Enter Sanur. My friend Karlie, founder of Bali Buddies, knows how to do Bali well. She moved to Sanur a decade ago. "Everyone thought I was daggy living in Sanur," she told me, laughing. The clients were in Seminyak and Canggu. The scene was elsewhere. "Now everyone wants to live here." Everyone thought I was daggy living in Sanur. Now everyone wants to live here. Foot massages for the family in Sanur. She says the reason Canggu became Canggu — the nightclubs, the construction, the relentless churn of new development — is partly because the local landowners in that area were historically less prosperous, and when developers came knocking, they sold. The Sanur locals were already well-established, already protective of their community, and they simply said no to a great deal of what Canggu said yes to. No nightclubs. No high-rises. No overnight transformation into a party destination. What remains is a place where actual Balinese and Indonesian people live their actual lives, and visitors are woven gently through rather than overwhelming the place entirely. Exploring Sanur with the kids. Add to this the fact that Sanur has no surf break — and therefore no surfer crowd, and therefore none of the scene that follows surfers from Legian to Seminyak to Canggu to Uluwatu in an endless migration — and you have an area that has, almost accidentally, remained itself. "It has a proper village vibe," Karlie said. "Nobody cares what you do or where you live. It is completely the opposite of Seminyak." She moved there for her children. She wanted them riding bikes along the beach path, not growing up in what she described, with admirable precision, as "the eastern suburbs of Bali." Dinner in Sanur with our feet in the sand. Walking around Sanur, I understood immediately. (If you are weighing up where to stay in Bali with kids, this is the area I would start with.) The beach path is wide and flat and lined with warungs and cafes, and people — local people, families, elderly couples, stray dogs of extraordinary variety — simply move through it in both directions all day long. The strip of cafes along the harbour near the port is excellent and unself-conscious. We had beach massages in the late afternoon, the kids chased dogs. It is easy breezy and beautiful and I am already thinking about going back. Bali Beach Hotel, The Heritage Collection Bali Beach Hotel: the grand dame and first high-rise in Sanur. We stayed…

articles.title: Everyone's Doing Breathwork. But Does It Actually Work?
articles.excerpt: Breathwork is having a real moment. But is it actually worth the hype, or is it just wellness theatre with a good soundtrack? We asked wellness expert Brooke Stevenson to walk us through the science, the techniques and how to start safely.
articles.body: Breathwork is having a real moment. But is it worth the hype, or is it just wellness theatre with a good soundtrack? We asked our Beauticate Collective wellness expert Brooke Stevenson to walk us through the science, the techniques and how to start safely. Brooke Stevenson, founder of Luxe Wellness and Beauticate Collective breathwork expert. Breathwork begins where movement meets stillness — learning to use your breath as a tool, not just a reflex. What Is Breathwork Actually Doing to Your Body? The short version. Your breath is one of the only parts of your nervous system you can control on purpose, and you can use it to dial yourself up or down. Brooke splits it into two camps. "I think of breathwork in two categories," she says. "Sympathetic, activating techniques use faster-paced breath to stimulate the body quickly. Parasympathetic, calming techniques slow everything down, typically through longer, slower breaths with extended exhales." Both do their work through the same channel. The vagus nerve. It is the longest nerve in the body, running from the brainstem through the heart, lungs and gut, and it is essentially the main cable of your rest-and-digest system. Here is where it gets convincing. A 2025 review of thirty studies on slow, diaphragmatic breathing found it lowers cortisol and improves vagal tone and emotional control, with effects that carry into how your body handles the next stressor. In practice that means breathing slowly at four to six breaths per minute reliably improves your heart rate variability, which is one of the cleanest markers we have of a resilient nervous system. Activating breath works in the opposite direction, and on purpose. "It deliberately stimulates a stress response, which the brain then registers and regulates," Brooke explains. That controlled hit of stress is part of how it builds resilience and helps release stored tension or emotion. Your breath is one of the only parts of your nervous system you can control on purpose — and you can use it to dial yourself up or down. There is a gut angle too. The vagus nerve signals in both directions between the brain and the gut, which is part of why people notice their digestion shifting alongside the calm. If you have ever wondered why anxiety, gut issues and chronic pain tend to travel together, this is the nerve that connects them. Either way, activating or calming, you are changing your biochemistry. Oxygenating cells, improving circulation, supporting mental clarity. The Main Breathwork Techniques, Explained Not all breathwork feels the same, and it helps to know roughly where a technique sits before you try it. On the activating end you have the fast, breath-holding or circular patterns. Think Wim Hof style breathing, holotropic and rebirthing. "They bring suppressed emotion or energy to the surface and create release," Brooke says. This is the camp that produces the big emotional moments you see online. On the calming end you have the slower, extended-exhale techniques. Resonance breathing, box breathing and the 4-2-6 pattern all live here. Their job is to restore a sense of safety and settle the body. Two beginner-friendly places to start. Box breathing is a steady square. Breathe in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four, and repeat. The 4-2-6 is even simpler and leans on the long exhale that does so much of the calming work. Breathe in for four, hold for two, out for six. The longer out-breath is the part that tells your nervous system it is safe to stand down. Setting the scene matters. articles.title: Cancer Changed My Beauty Routine… But More Than That, It Changed Me
articles.author: Beauticate Editorial
articles.excerpt: In her second piece for Beauticate, Colette Harvey picks up where she left off — through double mastectomy, lymph node surgery, chemotherapy, cold capping and radiation — and the quiet shift in what beauty has come to mean.
articles.body: Earlier this year, Colette Harvey let us into one of the most personal chapters of her life, a breast cancer diagnosis that arrived just before Christmas, at 43. A respected publicist and stylist, and one of Sigourney's oldest friends, she chose to tell her story publicly in the hope it might help even one woman. Her first piece moved thousands of readers. If you are new to Colette, I Got Breast Cancer for Christmas is where her story begins. Here, she picks up where she left off, through surgery, chemotherapy and a quiet shift in what beauty has come to mean. As I sat down to write my second article, I realised I had been putting it off. Not because I have not loved sharing my story or connecting with people who have reached out to share theirs. I think I was putting it off because, in some strange way, I was protecting myself. I wanted to get through chemotherapy first. I wanted to have a clearer picture — or at least as clear as one can have while still living through it — of what I wanted to say and how I truly felt. When the big C unexpectedly came into my life, I made myself a few promises: it was going to change my life for the better. Right at the top of that list was being completely honest about this journey. The good, the bad, the funny and the really bloody hard. When the big C came into my life, I made myself a few promises: it was going to change my life for the better. Since my first article, a lot has happened. After my double mastectomy, we discovered that the cancer had spread to my lymph nodes. Annoyingly, that meant another surgery just three weeks later to remove them all from my right side. I honestly thought losing my breasts would be the hardest part. Shockingly, it wasn't. What Nobody Tells You About Lymph Node Removal Nobody really prepares you for what happens when your lymph nodes are removed. Your lymphatic system no longer moves fluid around your body the way it once did, and suddenly I found myself with what I lovingly refer to as "tuck shop arms." Yes, that is now an official medical term in our house. Along with that came cording — a tight, painful pulling sensation that ran down the entire right-hand side of my body. It made even simple movements uncomfortable. Thankfully, my incredible surgeon armed me with exercises and rehabilitation techniques, and one of the greatest wins throughout this journey has been meeting Kate Perkins on the Central Coast. Kate specialises in all aspects of cancer rehabilitation and breast cancer related lymphoedema (BCRL), using state of the art technology to deliver photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) to minimise the side effects of cancer treatment, including reducing the development of radiation fibrosis, and minimising the development of BCRL, and speeding up recovery times. I have seen Kate twice a week since my surgery and, despite being considered high risk, I have thankfully avoided lymphoedema so far. Touch wood. Kate has become one of the many incredible people who have carried me through this journey. Chemotherapy, Cold Capping and a Very Elite Playlist Then came chemotherapy. I had my treatment at the SAN Hospital, where one of my oncologists is based, and you can bet your life I chose cold capping. If there was even a small chance I could keep my hair, I was taking it. I researched cold capping for weeks. I contacted the company that made the machines, watched…

articles.title: The Island That Saved Our Family Holiday
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Thirty minutes offshore, a world away. How Nusa Lembongan turned a fractious Bali family trip into the holiday we'll talk about for years.
articles.body: Three days into our first family trip to Bali, I am standing in a lane in Canggu watching my ten-year-old attempt to smuggle a street dog into our villa. Not a small, manageable dog. A large, amber-coloured, visibly flea-ridden dog who has adopted Lulu with the devotion of a long-lost relative. She has named her Lola. She is already negotiating terms. "We can put her in the luggage, Mum." I explain, for the third time that afternoon, about Australian quarantine laws. Lulu listens carefully. She does not accept the premise. Meanwhile, my fourteen-year-old and I have had more arguments than is comfortable about his urgent need to check his phone whenever he thinks I'm not looking. Canggu is extraordinary — the cafes, the rice paddies glimpsed between surf shops, the chaotic beautiful energy of it — but by day three, I have started to wonder if we are actually on holiday together or simply in the same time zone. This is why I had built Nusa Lembongan into the trip deliberately. Call it editorial instinct, or maternal self-preservation. Either way, I knew we needed it. I had handed the whole thing to The Lembongan Traveller, and they had taken it from there. The Crossing Our Rocky Fast Cruise departs Sanur at noon. The channel crossing takes thirty minutes of air-conditioned comfort in the lower cabin. I keep standing to steal glances out of the sea-spattered windows above us, the water shifting from grey-green to the kind of blue that doesn't look real — a saturated, almost electric turquoise that makes you reach for your phone to capture it even before you've arrived. The island appears slowly: limestone cliffs, coconut palms, a thin white line of beach. It looks like somewhere you'd find on a very optimistic screen saver. Lulu spots three dogs on the beach upon arrival. We move quickly. Villa Tranquilla The name is doing a great deal of work, and it earns every syllable. We are collected from the dock in an oversized buggy with padded seats in the back and driven up into Sandy Bay, through narrow lanes where high stone walls conceal whatever lives behind them. Ours is a grey wooden door, fairly unremarkable from the outside. Putu, the villa manager, is waiting to welcome us — warm, efficient, quietly amused by the general chaos of our arrival. We step through the door and the world opens. The entrance path is lined with marigold offerings and pandan trees forming a loose canopy overhead. Frangipani petals fall softly as we walk. Behind the bamboo-screened entrance, the villa unfolds into a vast outdoor living space: an enormous white daybed-sofa, beautifully carved timber table and bench seats, an open kitchen with beaded light fixtures, and beyond it all — the infinity pool, the Indian Ocean, the cliffs, the sky. The view is a 180-degree sweep across Teluk Uwung Bay. The water below is that same impossible blue. On the rocky headland to the right, another villa perches on the cliff edge like something from a film set. The sound, when you stop talking, is the Indian Ocean crashing against the limestone below, over and over, rhythmic and enormous and completely indifferent to anything you brought here to worry about. The sound, when you stop talking, is the Indian Ocean crashing against the limestone below, over and over, rhythmic and enormous and completely indifferent to anything you brought here to worry about. Damien and I stand there for a moment, not saying anything. The teenager puts his phone in his backpack. It stays there for the rest of the afternoon.…

articles.title: The Bali Resort That Solves the Family Holiday Dilemma
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Asia's first luxury all-inclusive resort just landed in Bali - and it might be the smartest family holiday you book this year.
articles.body: The best family resorts in Nusa Dua, Bali have always had a problem: they do families brilliantly, or they do adults beautifully, but rarely both at once. Paradisus by Meliá Bali - the newly transformed luxury all-inclusive resort on Nusa Dua's sherbet sands, and the first of its kind in Asia - is making a serious case for both. Sigourney checked in to see if it delivered. The Welcome Ceremony That Sets the Tone I close my eyes as the priest begins to chant. The air is thick with frangipani and incense. Smoke curls upwards through a canopy of coconut palms, dissipating into the morning light. Somewhere above us, birds chirrup and palm fronds clatter softly in the breeze. And then, my eye catches a swift movement above us: a squirrel darting up the ancient stone shrine, pausing for a moment as though he too has come to pay his respects. Kneeling in a sarong and sash on cobbled stone of the temple, I hold my canang sari - a small square tray I've just made (badly) from janur , young coconut palm leaves. Inside: grains of rice, petals of frangipani and marigold, a sliver of pandan, a slice of banana. The priest looks like he's seen decades of early mornings and open air. He has eyes that seem permanently on the verge of laughing at something only he can see. The other journalists bow their heads. I follow. Our welcome ceremony takes place in the gardens of Paradisus by Meliá Bali, which has just emerged from a significant renovation and is pitching itself as the ultimate Bali luxury family holiday. At this particular moment, though, none of that is the point. What strikes me is the silence within the sound. The chanting, the birds, the leaves - all of it present, layered, alive - and underneath it, a profound stillness. I haven't sat still like this for a very long time. After his incantation, the priest sits with us and speaks about Tri Hita Karana, the Balinese understanding of wellbeing as a balance between people, nature and the divine. Sekala and niskala , the seen world and the unseen. We are all connected, he says. What we put out returns to us. It's not a complex philosophy. It's also not one that's easy to remember when you're at home answering emails at ten-thirty at night. And yet, somewhere between the incense and the rustling of leaves, it lands. I walk away feeling calmer than I have in weeks. Somewhere between the incense and the rustling of leaves, it lands. I walk away feeling calmer than I have in weeks. Why Nusa Dua - and Why This Resort in Particular Located on the sherbet-sand peninsula of Nusa Dua - the name means "two islands" in Balinese, a nod to the two small headlands that define this southern coastline - Paradisus by Meliá Bali marks the brand's first foray into Asia. The resort draws its philosophy from what it calls Wellness Designed by Destination, which sounds exactly like the kind of phrase that should make a travel writer's eyes glaze over. Thankfully, it delivers considerably more than wellness buzzwords. Inside Paradisus: What 40 Years and a Full Renovation Looks Like The building that became Paradisus has more history than its fresh renovation might suggest. Meliá Bali opened in 1985 as the first Meliá hotel outside Spain: a Majorcan hospitality group betting on a stretch of southern Bali that had barely registered on the international tourist map. At the time, the area had not yet attained its later popularity. The resort that…

articles.title: Which Wellness Gadgets Are Worth Your Money?
articles.author: Camilla Thompson
articles.excerpt: Beauticate's Wellness Editor Camilla Thompson shares the three technologies she'd keep if she could only choose three - and the common mistake people make before they're ready.
articles.body: Beauticate's Wellness Editor Camilla Thompson shares the three technologies she'd keep if she could only choose three — and the common mistake people make before they're ready. Here's something the wellness technology industry doesn't often say out loud: most of it is trying to replicate what nature already does for free. Infrared light. Heat exposure. Cold immersion. Circadian rhythm regulation. Grounding. These aren't new biohacking discoveries - they're ancient biological inputs that our bodies were designed to receive and that modern life has largely removed. The technology exists to fill that gap and, often, it does so remarkably well. But before you invest in a single device, the most powerful thing you can do is get yourself outside. Morning light. Bare feet on grass. Ocean swims. Movement in fresh air. Not as a warm-up act to the real protocol, but as the foundation of it. The research on nature exposure for cortisol regulation, sleep quality, immune function and mental health is as strong as almost anything in the biohacking space. It's just harder to sell. When you're getting those inputs consistently, you'll get significantly more out of the technology. It amplifies what nature starts. Something else I've come to believe is that the most valuable wellness technologies aren't just tools - they're rituals. Before investing in anything, I ask myself a simple question: will this become a meaningful part of my day? A device you use consistently as an intentional pause, a moment of stillness, breath or recovery, will always outperform one that sits on a shelf waiting for the perfect moment. With that in mind, if I could only keep three wellness technologies, they would be my infrared sauna, red light therapy device and a wearable tracker. Infrared Sauna My sauna gets used every second day and has become one of my non-negotiables. I love it for relaxation, stress reduction, recovery and longevity. It's one of the few wellness technologies with a substantial body of research behind it, including the landmark Finnish sauna studies, which found regular sauna use was associated with a significantly reduced risk of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality. We're talking about a technology that may genuinely support a longer, healthier life. The fact that you feel incredible afterwards is simply an added bonus. Beyond longevity, I love saunas for women because they create a dedicated space to slow down. Many of us spend our days in constant output mode - working, caregiving, managing households and looking after everyone else. Twenty minutes in a sauna becomes less about the heat and more about creating space to pause, breathe and reconnect. If you don't have a home sauna, booking into a dedicated infrared sauna studio is a great starting point and worth doing before investing in your own. If you're ready for home use, Clearlight and FoundSpace make some of the most considered options available. For a more accessible entry point, a portable infrared dome delivers many of the same benefits and can be packed away when not in use. Red Light Therapy My red light therapy device would be a close second. I use it regularly and love that it's simple, accessible and easy to integrate into daily life. The research around skin health, recovery, inflammation and mitochondrial function continues to grow, making it one of the more versatile wellness tools available. My preference is a full-body panel over a mask because it provides greater coverage and higher irradiance. BON CHARGE makes full-panel options I'd recommend without hesitation and has been transparent about its technology in a market that isn't always. What I love most about…

articles.title: What Nobody Told Me About My Body After 40, and Why I Had to Find Out Myself
articles.author: Lisa Walker
articles.excerpt: Eir Women co-founder Lisa Walker on perimenopause, creatine, the research that shocked her - and what she wishes someone had told her before 40.
articles.body: There was a moment, somewhere in my early forties, when I realised that everything had simply stopped working. It was gradual, and it snuck up, tapping me on the shoulder when I wasn't quite ready. The workouts that used to keep me lean weren't working anymore. I was eating better than ever but still bloated. Sleep was a joke. My mood was, let's say, not my finest. And the people closest to me were noticing. I wasn't the same person. It was during Covid that I really started talking about it properly with my business partner Kate. We'd been spending so much time together we couldn't blame stress alone. After many walks and many conversations, we started digging. I grew up with a naturopath mother. Kate had a GP father. We started asking questions. What we found shocked us. And eventually, it changed everything. Nobody was talking about it. And the odd occasion they were, nobody was listening. The first thing that hit me was how dismissed women were. The products on the market were clearly not designed by women like us. The supplement category was overwhelming and largely useless. And perimenopause! This years-long transition that precedes menopause, was barely spoken about at all. When it was, it was framed as something to simply endure. Symptoms like fatigue, brain fog, weight gain, low mood and disrupted sleep were being written off as 'simply getting older.' Women were gaslit by doctors and being told to 'just deal with it'. That was what made me truly angry. Women were gaslit by doctors and being told to 'just deal with it'. And we weren't alone. Research Eir Women conducted across 322 Australian women aged 40 to 60 found that 62% felt under-informed about how perimenopause and menopause affect metabolism and weight, with many expressing frustration at the absence of guidance on what to actually do about it. Nearly a third of women aged 41 to 50 strongly agreed they felt overwhelmed. Not occasionally, but as a baseline state of being. It's a systemic failing that hits 50% of our population. So we went deep. Kate and I spent years in the research before Eir Women existed as a brand. Three years, in fact. We were not interested in what was trending. We were interested in what worked. And what we kept coming back to was this: the underlying systems: sleep, stress response, adrenal function and energy production needed support. Women needed consistent, evidence-based support over 'miracle cures'. Every ingredient in our formulations is there for a specific reason, backed by at least three clinical papers and dosed at the levels those papers identified as effective. No fairy-dust quantities designed to look impressive on a label. No more than ten ingredients per product. Efficacy, not marketing. One of the ingredients I'm most passionate about is creatine. I know, you might associate it with gym bros wanting to bulk up. But for women over 40, dosed at 5g daily, creatine supports muscle mass, brain function, cellular energy production, and even bone health. It's one of the most researched compounds available, and most women have never even considered it. That gap between the evidence and the public conversation is exactly the problem we set out to close. Take creatine daily to help with muscle mass, brain health and even bone health. What actually moves the needle, and what doesn't. The biggest mistake I see women making in their forties is thinking they need to try harder. More workouts. Less food. More discipline. In reality, that approach often makes things worse. More stress, more cortisol, more hormonal…

articles.title: Welcome to the New Beauticate and Our Shop
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: The question I get asked most is always the same: just tell me what to buy. So we built a shop, rebuilt the website, and here's everything that's new.
articles.body: The question I get is always some version of the same thing: "just tell me what to buy." There's a question I get asked constantly. In DMs, in WhatsApp chats, at dinner parties, at school pickup. Sometimes from strangers, sometimes from women I've known for twenty years. The question is always some version of the same thing: just tell me what to buy. They don't want a mood board or a list of forty things they'll screenshot and never look at again. They want to know what I would actually choose. The LED mask I'd actually buy. The candle that's actually worth it. The fragrance that's been sitting on my bathroom shelf for three years, not because I forgot about it, but because I keep reaching for it. I've been writing about beauty and wellness for twenty-six years. My first beauty writing gig was at an indie magazine called Your Destiny when I was 18. From there, TV Week , where I had my own beauty and fashion page (and where I once had to rub bronzing cream on Chris Hemsworth's chest during a cover shoot because the makeup artist had gone home. True story.) Then New Woman , then Glamour , then Vogue Australia for the better part of a decade. Then Beauticate, which I founded in 2014 because I wanted to build something more personal than a magazine and more honest than the algorithm-driven beauty internet we were all starting to drown in. And for all of that time, the most useful thing I have apparently ever done is be the person my friends text when they need to know where to buy a good candle. So we built a shop. Then we rebuilt the entire website. Let me show you what's new. 01 — Beauticate Shop This is where it all started. An edit of beauty, wellness and lifestyle products I actually use and believe in, with every order fulfilled directly by the brand. Nothing is here because someone paid for placement. Everything is here because it has earned its spot. The launch lineup includes fragrance from Lumira and Tulita, Australian botanical skincare from Mukti Organics, wellness from JS Health and Eir Women, skin from SaintLouve, La Mav and Subtle Energies, and one of my all-time favourite lifestyle brands, Maison Balzac. You can shop by category, by brand, or by moment: the Deepest Sleep edit, the Winter Edit, Self-Care Sunday. A shop that thinks the way I think. I've got some seriously exciting skincare and wellness brands coming — it's just working through the various levels of their business to get them onboarded that takes time. But I can't wait to share as they join. And then I'll be adding more brands to Style (think wardrobe staples for real life), plus Living (great things for your home) and Travel (everything you need to pack to stay sane). But the shop is only part of what's new. We rebuilt the entire site, and there's a lot to explore. 02 — Ask Sig An AI-powered beauty and wellness concierge that draws on twelve years of Beauticate editorial. Ask it anything, any time. 03 — Beautiful Inside Podcast Hub The podcast has a proper home now, with a mood-based filter — browse by what you're going through, not just by episode number. 04 — Destinations Travel curated by feeling: Girls Trip, Reset and Heal, Switch Off, Explore a City, Family Adventure, Romantic Escapes. 05 — The Beauty and Wellness Directory A searchable directory of spas, salons, skin clinics, bathhouses, retreats and wellness venues across Australia. 06 — About Beauticate and…

articles.title: Sacred Six for Stress and Sanity
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: I have spent the past year quietly building a whole new chapter of Beauticate. It has been creative and fulfilling and, if I am honest, the most stressful season of my life. These are the six rituals keeping me sane.
articles.body: Listen to the full episode here Why Stress Management Matters Now I am writing this with a knot in my shoulder and a to-do list that refuses to end. Over the past year I have been quietly building a whole new chapter of Beauticate. It has been exciting, creative and deeply fulfilling. It has also, if I am honest, been the most stressful stretch of my life. So in this solo Sacred Six episode I am not theorising. I am handing over the six rituals, tools and practices that have actually kept me grounded, regulated my nervous system and protected my wellbeing through long workdays, chronic pain, anxiety and the kind of overwhelm that creeps up before you notice it. If you have been feeling stretched too thin, sleeping badly or simply trying to hold everything together, this one is for you. Small rituals, I have learned, do the heavy lifting. Infrared Sauna, Walks and Breathwork This is my non-negotiable. Twenty minutes in an infrared sauna and my whole body downshifts. The chatter quietens, the tension in my neck loosens, and I sleep better that night. It has become my reset for stress, sleep and chronic pain all at once. I use the Nook Infrared Sauna at home, and the code BEAUTICATE will sort you out if you want one of your own. Small rituals, I have learned, do the heavy lifting. When my head is loudest, the answer is rarely to be alone with it. A walk with a friend does what no app can. We move, we talk, we offload, and somewhere around the second kilometre everything feels more manageable. The research on community and mental health is clear, but you feel it long before you read it. We started a Beauticate Walk and Talk WhatsApp group for exactly this, so come and walk with us. I came to breathwork sceptical and left a convert. A single 9D session with Brooke Stephenson at Luxe Wellness Collective moved something I had been carrying for months. Your breath is the fastest, cheapest, most portable tool you own for changing your state, and most of us are barely using it. Meditation, Massage and Vagus Nerve Tools This is the ritual I have relied on the longest. Most nights I stack a guided meditation onto my wind-down, either in the sauna or while wearing my LED mask (beautifying and relaxing, killing two birds). I pair my San Lueur LED mask with a guided meditation from Insight Timer, which is free and has a meditation for every mood, anxiety, insomnia, the lot. If you struggle with sleep, try their yoga nidra tracks. I love Jennifer Piercy and David Ji. Chronic neck and back tension is the physical face of my stress, and a heated massage is the quickest relief I have found. My Kiicity neck massager lives within arm's reach of my desk and earns its place every single day, and you can now find it in our shop. This is the surprise of the lot. The Pulsetto is a small wearable that gently stimulates the vagus nerve, and it has become a daily non-negotiable for calming stress, anxiety and the racing mind before sleep. Beauticate listeners can use the code BEAUTICATE for 15 per cent off. Building Your Own Stress Relief Kit None of these are a cure. They are a kit. And on the days everything feels like too much, having the kit ready is what gets me through. If this episode helped, I would be so grateful if you left a review, rated the podcast and shared it with a…

articles.title: The Brow Mistakes Most Women Make - and How to Fix Them
articles.author: Simone Aspinall
articles.excerpt: Our resident makeup artist and brow whisperer Simone Aspinall on using your brows to your advantage.
articles.body: There are certain areas of the face where getting it wrong costs you more than getting it right ever earns you. Brows are one of them. A well-groomed, well-shaped brow can lift the entire face, brighten the eyes and shave years off your appearance. An over-tweezed, poorly shaped or neglected one can do exactly the opposite. For women in their 40s and 50s dealing with thinning brows, patchy growth, greying hairs or the long-term fallout of a particularly aggressive ’90s waxing phase, working out where to even start can feel overwhelming. And it’s something that makeup artist and beauty therapist Simone Aspinall sees every day. The trick is not about chasing trends or creating a completely different shape, she says, but rather, it’s about enhancing what’s already there and creating balance, softness and structure in a way that looks effortless. Here, she breaks down the mistakes she sees most often, and exactly what to do instead. The single biggest brow mistake women over 40 make If you grew up in the ’90s, your brows may still be paying the price. “The biggest brow mistake I still see is over-thinning,” says Simone. “Women in their 40s and 50s lived through the ’90s brow era, and unfortunately years of over-plucking and waxing can permanently damage the follicle.” The compounding issue is that brows naturally thin as we age anyway. Taking them too fine accelerates the effect. “It can instantly make the face appear harsher and less youthful,” she says. Her advice? Step away from the tweezers. “I almost never recommend going thinner with brows. A softly structured, fuller brow is far more flattering because it frames the eyes, creates lift and brings balance back to the face.” The goal she’s working towards isn’t an Instagram brow or anything heavily laminated. “It’s simply a healthy, polished brow with enough fullness to create definition while still looking natural.” A softly structured, fuller brow is far more flattering because it frames the eyes, creates lift and brings balance back to the face. Why colour matters more than you think Here’s one that gets overlooked constantly. As we age, brow hairs don’t just thin, they lose pigment too. They go grey, wiry and less defined. And when the brows fade, everything around the eyes loses definition. “Even the most subtle tint can make an enormous difference,” says Simone. “You don’t need dark brows, but adding a soft wash of colour helps create fullness, structure and definition around the eyes without looking obvious.” A professional tint is a simple, low-commitment treatment that delivers outsized results. If you haven’t tried it, add it to your next salon visit. And if you don’t like fiddling with brow pencils or powder, BOOIE has you covered with Bring Back the Bush — a highly pigmented tinted gel that gives colour, shape and volume to sparse brows in one swipe. It’s the low-effort, high-payoff option. The shape mistake that drags your face down You can have perfectly full, well-tinted brows and still be ageing yourself with the wrong shape. Specifically: a tail that drops too low. “When the tail of the brow extends too far downward towards the cheekbone, it can visually drag the face down,” says Simone. “One of the simplest ways to create a fresher look is by keeping the brow slightly lifted and balanced. A gentle arch through the highest point of the brow and a clean, well-positioned tail can instantly brighten the eye area.” If you’re unsure whether yours are sitting in the right place, it’s worth booking a professional shaping appointment rather than attempting corrections at home.…

articles.title: Why Giving Back Became Non-Negotiable
articles.author: Shentel Lee
articles.excerpt: Beauticate’s Culture Editor who accidentally founded a food bank on how giving back will save you too.
articles.body: Some people talk about purpose. Shentel Lee built an NGO, a community centre and a food bank from her phone. Beauticate's Culture Editor - designer, entrepreneur and one of Tatler Asia's Most Influential women - writes on why giving back stopped being optional, and what it actually looks like when the cameras aren't rolling. Beauticate’s Culture Editor who accidentally founded a food bank on how giving back will save you too. The word "giving" is complicated when your job is basically to take. I make things. I sell things. And I quietly siphon people's most precious resource: their attention. When a school mum tells me she saw my latest Reel, my reflex is still to wince. I know I overshare. I know I can be a lot. I am also comfortable admitting I have survived a full mental breakdown from burnout, that it takes daily work to put my mental health first, and that I still neglect myself enough to edge back towards what I call the black hole. Somewhere along the way, though, this noisy little corner of the internet stopped being just a shop window. It became the engine room for the work I am proudest of. The space you step into when you scroll my feed now helps keep families fed in Kuching. If you are here, you are already part of it. How it started: a pandemic, a message, and a snap decision Five years ago, deep in the first wave of COVID, I opened a message on Instagram asking for help. Families in Kuching could not access basic things like masks and hand sanitiser. We were already in grief after my father-in-law had passed away. I could easily have scrolled past. I did not. Something snapped into focus. It felt like being yanked out of quicksand. I knew suppliers, I knew who to call, and I knew there were people in my community who would help if I gave them a way to do it. Daily updates from my phone reached people stuck at home who desperately wanted to do something but did not know where to start. They donated. They shared. And I realised I could use the space I had built as a direct line to give back. That first mission changed everything. Giving back will ask something of you. But it will also give you a clarity and a grounding that are very hard to find anywhere else. What Kuching Food Aid actually looks like (it's not glamorous) Today I am a full-time volunteer at Kuching Food Aid, an NGO I accidentally founded because donors believed in the transparency of what I was sharing. We are not traditional. Our meetings happen in WhatsApp chats and video calls. Volunteers send photos, numbers and names through their phones. Donors can message me directly and get every image and piece of data they need, without sitting through long, expensive meetings. We have no admin or logistics fees. Every ringgit goes directly to food aid. My service does not look like what people might imagine. It is spreadsheets and invoices, coordinating food orders, chasing name lists and photos, updating donors, and tracking expenses from my laptop and phone. It is not photogenic. But it gives me a depth of purpose I cannot find anywhere else. In 2023, my husband Dato Bobby Ting and I opened the Kuching Community Social Support Centre in the heart of the city, bringing NGOs and government welfare agencies together under one roof. More than 1,000 patrons now come through monthly. It is, I think, the most practical thing I have ever…

articles.title: Where Family Memories Are Made
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: How Wild Luxury's Crane Lodge and Calabash Bay Lodge became part of our family's story.
articles.body: There are not many places that can comfortably host three generations of a family, a long birthday lunch, a dozen excited children in pyjamas and a group of mothers drinking wine around a fire pit.Wild Luxury's Crane Lodge and Calabash Bay Lodge can. Over the years we've stayed at both properties in wildly different configurations. A multi-generational family gathering. A weekend away with Damien's parents. A mummy-and-daughter birthday sleepover for Lulu and her closest friends. And somehow, despite the shifting cast of characters, both lodges delivered the same thing every time: space to connect. Not just physically, but emotionally. The fact that they're also beautifully designed, deeply sustainable and set in some of New South Wales' most spectacular landscapes feels almost secondary. The new language of sustainable luxury travel in Australia doesn’t announce itself. It doesn’t ask for sacrifice or applause. It simply shows up in how a place is built, how it sits in the landscape, and how it allows people to gather, rest and reconnect without friction. That’s what I felt so clearly across two stays with Wild Luxury . If you’ve followed our approach to design-led travel – you’ll understand this lens. This wasn’t about escape. It was about how a place holds real life. And not solo, not romantically, not even quietly. These were stays with my extended family – which, for many families, requires a certain kind of house: with places to assemble but also enough spaces for time apart. A retreat for the in-laws far from the maddening cries of kids. Built for moments of peace and solitude that every parent craves. Crane Lodge: a treehouse for everyone we love Crane Lodge was our first chapter, and in many ways, the most layered. Perched high above Pittwater on Garigal Country, the arrival itself sets the tone. You step into the inclinator and glide slowly up through the bush, past spotted gums and dense greenery, leaving the road and its urgency behind. By the time you step off, you already feel recalibrated. That weekend we invited our whole family – all three sets of grandparents and my brothers for a special lunch. A true multi-generational gathering. The house held us effortlessly. No one felt on top of each other, yet no one felt removed. There are moments when good architecture does emotional labour for you, and this is one of them. There are moments when good architecture does emotional labour for you, and this is one of them. The design details reveal themselves slowly. Blonde timber, terrazzo surfaces, custom ceramics, woollen cushions in soft, earthy tones. Large sliding windows that open the house completely to the forest so you can quite literally sleep and bathe among the trees. The artwork matters too: considered Australian pieces that feel in dialogue with the landscape rather than imposed upon it. Outside, the property unfolds like a series of invitations. A curved pool surrounded by a very chic steel post fence. A cedar hot tub hidden among greenery. A fire pit framed by cathedral-like stone, where conversations stretch longer than planned. Hammocks, swinging chairs, a yoga deck. Quiet corners that somehow always seem to be free when you need them. The next time we stayed, the tone shifted completely and the house met us there too. We hosted Lulu’s birthday at Crane Lodge, inviting her closest friends and their mums, who also happen to be my good friends. We did a mummy/daughter sleepover. Children in pyjamas running between rooms. Laughter echoing through the house. Parents lingering over wine while keeping one eye on the chaos. It could have felt…

articles.title: Everything We're Buying for Winter
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Coats, creams and candles our editors can’t stop buying.
articles.body: As the weather cools and the light softens, so do the things we reach for. The Beauticate Winter edit is a curated mix of richer textures, warmer tones and more considered layers. From fragrance to fashion and the small rituals in between, these are the autumn pieces the Beauticate team is loving right now. The Pieces We’re Reaching for Right Now "Winter always makes me gravitate towards pieces that feel a little more structured and tactile. And I love the sharp, sculptural feel of a great blazer. It instantly pulls everything together. So, it becomes an easy foundation for everything else. Also, a small flash of gold, like a softly scalloped hoop earring, catches the light through hair and adds that subtle polish. Fragrance-wise, I’ve been wearing Goldfield & Banks Purple Suede constantly. It’s smoky, woody, a little bit sexy. The kind of scent that lingers on knits and scarves. When my skin inevitably starts to feel dry or slightly irritated, Mukti Marigold Cream is deeply nourishing and the scent makes it feel like a proper ritual . Also, I've been leaning into texture more this season. A woven leather shoe, something slightly unexpected, can add an extra element of interest." “Chocolate brown is having a moment and I’m embracing it. It feels softer than black but just as polished, and works beautifully layered tone-on-tone. I’ve been living in cosy, elevated staples that instantly make you feel put-together. A great coat is non-negotiable for winter. It’s the hero piece you build every outfit around. I love timeless, flattering styles that are easy to throw over anything and instantly elevate even the simplest look. A white or cream base layer is the foundation of so many outfits, whether worn on its own or layered under knits and coats. Look for pieces that feel warm without bulk and pair effortlessly with everything. I’ve also been leaning into richer, earthy tones at home. Think terracotta, sienna and warm clay hues that instantly make a space feel more inviting as the weather cools. It’s such an easy way to transition interiors into winter with minimal effort but maximum impact. As the temperature drops, I also switch to richer, more nourishing skincare. It’s all about skin feeling comforted and radiant by morning.” “In the cooler months, I naturally gravitate towards pieces and rituals that feel warm, functional and effortless. I tend to carry more in winter, whether it’s extra makeup, layers or just life in general, so I love beautiful accessories that are also practical for travel and everyday use. At home, I’m drawn to fragrance that makes a space feel cosy and calming without being overpowering. I’ve always preferred room sprays and simple scent rituals that feel clean, minimal and easy to use. For skin, protection becomes everything in winter. I look for products that help lock in hydration while shielding the skin from environmental stress like wind and dryness, without feeling heavy. And even in cooler weather, SPF is non-negotiable. I want formulas that feel elegant, lightweight and completely invisible on the skin." "This is the season where I lean into softness and care, both in beauty and in how I look after myself. My style becomes more refined, but never overdone. Effortless, considered, easy to wear. I find myself reaching for pieces like the Bec + Bridge Laurent Set. Polished, understated, quietly confident. I become focused on the small shifts that make a difference. A chocolate-toned mascara instead of black. Warmer, softer, more modern. My routine becomes more intentional too. Scalp care moves to the top of my list, and right now…

articles.title: I Never Thought I’d Enjoy Vacuuming and Then This Happened
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A vacuum that talks back, reveals invisible dust and somehow made me enjoy cleaning. My honest review of the Dyson V16 Submarine.
articles.body: I have always loved my Dyson. Genuinely loved it - not in the way you say you love something that works fine, but in the way you defend a brand to friends who suggest you try something else. This Dyson V16 review began when I was invited to the Dyson V16 launch and finally got to see what the newer technology could actually do. My old model was ancient - loyal but tired - so I jumped at the chance to take one home and give it a proper, honest go. Reader, it broke me. In the best possible way. If this Dyson V16 review proves anything, it is that I never thought I’d enjoy vacuuming. Let alone want to actually clean the damn thing. Yet suddenly, here I am, one Thursday night, lovingly taking it apart and detailing it with an old toothbrush, and, strangely, not minding one little bit. This is not who I used to be. Vacuum maintenance was always my hard no. The worst job in the house. The scissors. The hair. The gag reflex. The sense that I was wasting my one precious life dealing with something that should have worked better in the first place. But this machine changed the dynamic. That is really the heart of this Dyson V16 review: this machine removed the friction from a job I had always hated. The Dyson V16 Piston Animal Submarine quietly turned a job I loathed into something I… enjoy. Deeply. Repeatedly. Possibly too much. Dyson V16 review: the vacuum that talks back What makes this Dyson different isn’t just power (although yes, it has a lot of that). It’s the feedback. The laser alone deserves its own love letter. A precisely angled green beam reveals dust you genuinely cannot see with the naked eye: cat hair, crumbs, fine grit… all suddenly illuminated like evidence. Once you’ve seen it, you must clean it. Not because you’re a neat freak, but because the machine invites you to finish the job properly. Then there’s the LCD screen. As you vacuum, it shows exactly what you’re picking up, measured in microns, updating in real time. When you hit a filthy patch, the screen goes red and the vacuum works harder. As the floor gets cleaner, it moves through orange to green. A literal traffic-light system for cleanliness. At my recent birthday party, I just maybe, might have demonstrated this feature to several bemused friends after several rosés. If only Dyson was Avon I would have earned my commission ten-fold that night. For a time-poor woman juggling kids, pets and life, and for anyone with a slightly dopamine-hungry brain (hello fellow ADHD peeps, I see you), this is wildly satisfying. There’s proof. Closure. You know when you’re done Dyson V16 review: why I stopped hating vacuum maintenance Let’s talk about hair. Long hair. Pet hair. The kind that used to require scissors, swearing and a mild existential crisis. The V16’s anti-tangle technology uses two rotating conical brush bars that guide hair (up to 25 inches) straight into the bin. No wrapping. No cutting. No punishment for having a shedding cat or a family with heads attached. This is why I didn’t dread cleaning the vacuum. This is why I was oddly gentle with it. Maintenance no longer feels like a penalty, it feels intentional. Add to that the CleanCompaktor™ bin, which compresses dust as you go and holds up to 30 days’ worth before needing to be emptied. When you do empty it, it’s wipe-clean. No dusty clouds. No tangled surprises. No rage. Power where it counts (and knows…

articles.title: Sigourney's Sleep Edit (What Actually Helps)
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: The exact products I rely on when sleep isn’t perfect but still needs to happen.
articles.body: Sleep is an enigma but oh-so-important. If you’re anything like me, it doesn’t always come easily. There are nights when your brain just… won’t switch off. You open your notes to jot one thing down and suddenly you’re sliding into a casual doom-scroll until 2am. And then there are those evenings I go to bed early feeling quietly smug, only to wake at 4am thinking about something I said in 2007. This edit isn’t about an ideal routine. It’s about the sleep-enhancers I actually use to wind down, stay asleep and wake up feeling like myself again Sleep isn’t a luxury. It’s the foundation of everything — skin, mood, energy, resilience. Sleep isn’t a luxury. It’s the foundation of everything — skin, mood, energy, resilience. This edit brings together the pieces we reach for when we need to truly reset: calming rituals, nervous system support and deeply nourishing night care. From weighted comfort and soft candlelight to targeted supplements and overnight skincare that works while you rest. Nothing complicated — just the essentials that help you switch off, stay asleep and wake up feeling like yourself again. These are the ones that make a difference.

articles.title: The One Thing Missing from Your Skincare Routine Isn't a Serum
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Three masks. Three real-life moments. Sigourney shares her best skin reset.
articles.body: Skin is rarely static. It changes with stress, hormones, sleep, seasons and the countless invisible pressures we carry through our days. Yet many of us still approach skincare as though our complexion should behave exactly the same way every morning. Perimenopause has a way of rewriting that script. Faced with skin that could feel reactive one week, congested the next and perpetually tired somewhere in between, Beauticate publisher Sigourney found herself letting go of rigid routines in favour of something more intuitive. Here, she shares how three Jurlique masks found their place in everyday wellness rituals, helping her respond to stressed, hormonal and tired skin exactly when it needed it most. Three masks. Three real-life moments. Ten minutes each. This is what my skin reset actually looks like right now. I'm going to be honest with you. My skin has been a lot lately. I'm in the thick of perimenopause , running a business I'm about to launch a whole new arm of, raising a teenage boy who gives me daily heart attacks and a social butterfly daughter who requires approximately 400 lifts per week. I'm on my laptop by 6am. I'm answering emails in the car park. I'm making decisions all day long and by the time I get to myself, there's nothing left. And it has been showing up on my face. Not dramatically. More in that quiet, accumulative way. A little more reactive than usual. A little dull. Hormonal congestion along my jaw that wasn't there a few years ago. That vague feeling that my skin is tired. Like me. I'd been reaching for more. More serums, more actives, more steps. It didn't help. It just became another thing on the list. What I actually needed was less. But smarter. The Problem with a "Routine" We talk about skincare routines like our skin is the same every single day. It's not. Stress spikes sebum. Poor sleep tanks hydration. Hormones rewrite the whole script week to week. So why do we treat our skin like it has one fixed need? The answer came, unexpectedly, in the form of three tubes from Jurlique . The Australian brand has been growing biodynamic botanicals on its farm in the Adelaide Hills since 1985 and is one of the most trusted names in natural skincare. They've launched three new masks, each created to cater and customise to your skin's mood. you choose based on what your skin actually needs today. Not what your routine dictates. What your skin is asking for right now. I've been using all three. In three very specific, very real-life moments that I did not plan but could not have styled better if I'd tried. What I didn't expect was how perfectly they'd slot into something I'd already been quietly building. Over the past few months I've been deliberately creating little wellness pockets at home. Tiny infrastructure for decompression that I can actually access during a working day that would otherwise swallow me whole. The infrared sauna on the front doorstep. Reconciling my Xero accounts by the pool under the gum trees. Heading to the swing chair in the garden with my headphones to edit the podcast. Nothing elaborate. Just intentional. These three masks found their way into my routine as if they were designed for exactly that. Which, in a way, they were. Yes, I am one of those people who works by the pool as much as possible. Not because I'm relaxed. Because I am trying to trick my nervous system into thinking I am. This is where the Soothing Water-Cream Mask comes in. It's a…

articles.title: Meet the Beauticate Collective
articles.author: Beauticate Editorial
articles.excerpt: Meet the Beauticate Collective – a curated network of editors, experts and tastemakers shaping beauty, wellness, style and modern living.
articles.body: Meet The Beauticate Collective - a curated network of editors, experts and tastemakers shaping beauty, wellness, style and modern living. These are the women redefining what trusted recommendations look like now. There's something quietly powerful about a trusted recommendation. Not the kind that shouts. The kind that lands softly. The one you save, screenshot, and come back to. At Beauticate , that has always been the goal. To cut through the noise and bring you what actually works. What's worth your time. What feels good, not just looks good. Building this platform has been, among many things, a long and deliberate search for the right women to be part of it. Some I met in the magazine world over two decades ago. Some I discovered through their work. Some have been in my life for so long that formalising it almost feels funny: Mon has been colouring my hair for five years, Kristin has been styling Beauticate shoots for nearly a decade, and Kate , Rae and Jocelyn were among the very first women I interviewed for Beauticate, twelve years ago, when all of this was still a passion project I was building after hours at Vogue. What we are announcing today is not an influencer program. Nor is it a paid partnership arrangement dressed up as editorial. It’s something I’ve been quietly building toward for years. The Beauticate Collective is a curated group of editors, experts and tastemakers. Women at the top of their fields whose opinions carry weight because they have lived it, tested it and refined it over years, not weeks. Not built on follower count – built on credibility, taste and trust. Think of it as an extension of Beauticate’s editorial voice: a network of contributors who will share personal product edits, expert features, their real routines and rituals, and help shape what lands in the Beauticate.Shop (Eeep! More on that soon!). I am so excited for this. I hope you love The Collective as much as I do. Sigourney x Kate Waterhouse Kate was one of the very first women I ever interviewed on Beauticate, twelve years ago (and then again just a few months ago). Effortless, polished, always one step ahead – and, it turns out, completely one of us. She once tried to squeeze a laser facial between hosting sessions at a major fashion event. Sprinted there in full glam. The technician sent her straight back. “Honestly, the confidence I had in that plan is concerning,” she says dryly. Her mornings, by her own admission, are chaos: pyjamas, the dog, the garden, lunchboxes, school run.“It’s not giving ‘wellness morning routine.’ It’s giving survival mode.” Rae Morris Another of the OG Beauticate beauties and one of the first makeup artists I interviewed when I became a beauty editor over 20 years ago. Four-time Makeup Artist of the Year, bestselling author, known for her skin-first approach – and, it turns out, a brilliant storyteller. She once got veneers without fully understanding the filing process involved. The temporaries arrived looking like, in her words, “luminous yellow piano keys.” They fell off on day one of a major shoot. “It remains one of the more humbling moments of my career.” On feeling beautiful now: “Kindness – always – is the most beautiful thing. I really wish I’d known that earlier.” Jocelyn Petroni Joss used to look after my skin when I was at Vogue and when I first went to shoot her for Beauticate over 12 years ago ( read our latest chat ). I was in awe of her polished style and home. It always struck…

articles.title: Dr Sarah Jane on Trauma and Trusting the Body
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Dr Sarah Jane, the chiropractor and counsellor behind Spinal Energetics, joins me to talk about how the body holds trauma, why talk therapy alone is not always enough, and the lived experience that led her to a more embodied way of healing.
articles.body: Listen to the full episode here This week I am joined by Dr Sarah Jane, the holistic chiropractor and counsellor behind Spinal Energetics, and one of the most fascinating voices I have encountered at the intersection of science, somatics and the unseen. What struck me most about Sarah is not just the work she does. It is the life she has lived to arrive there. The life that led her here From a traumatic car accident and chronic pain, to an abusive relationship that left her body holding what her mind could not process, to years of fibromyalgia, miscarriages and navigating her mother's sudden brain injury, her story is layered, complex and deeply human. It is this lived experience that led her to a radical realisation. Healing is not just cognitive. It is physical, emotional and deeply embodied. When the body keeps score In this conversation we explore what happens when the body keeps score, why talk therapy alone is not always enough, and how creating safety in the nervous system can begin to shift even the deepest patterns. Sarah opens up about the concept of bracing, the unconscious tension so many of us carry, and why the goal is not to eliminate it, but to retrain it. As she beautifully explains, healing is not about never feeling pain again. It is about changing your relationship to it. Healing is not about never feeling pain again. It is about changing your relationship to it. Grief with no clear ending We also talk about grief that has no clear ending, miscarriages, identity loss and what she calls ambiguous grief, and why our culture still struggles to hold space for it. Her book Your Spine Holds the Answer launches in July, a guide to holistic healing, the emotional roots of pain, and Spinal Energetics. In this episode you will learn - Why your body can hold onto trauma long after your mind has processed it. - The difference between understanding healing and actually embodying it. - How bracing shows up in everyday life, and how to soften it. - Why emotional pain often lingers longer than physical pain. - The rituals and practices that helped Sarah rebuild herself, piece by piece. This is a conversation about resilience, but not the glossy kind. The real kind. The quiet kind. The kind that asks you to sit with yourself and, slowly and gently, come home. For more podcast chats like this, see Pip Edwards and Mukti Organics founder, Mukti.
