articles.title: 1 Hotel Melbourne Review: The Wellness Hotel Changing City Stays
articles.author: Beauticate Editorial
articles.excerpt: A new kind of city stay. At 1 Hotel Melbourne, biophilic design, Bamford spa rituals and thoughtful wellness touches turn travel into something restorative.
articles.body: A new kind of city stay has arrived. In this 1 Hotel Melbourne review, biophilic design, Bamford spa rituals and thoughtful wellness touches turn even a work trip into a restorative escape. A New Kind of Wellness Hotel in Melbourne There is a certain kind of city hotel that asks you to admire it. Then there is 1 Hotel Melbourne , which seems to exhale the moment you walk in. Outside, the bones are unmistakably urban. Steel, concrete, river, history. The Yarra slips past. The CBD hums nearby. Set on 220 metres of waterfront in the revived North Wharf precinct, the hotel rises from the old Seafarers wharf, its heart still beating inside Goods Shed No. 5, the last surviving heritage goods shed from Melbourne’s shipping heyday. Inside, though, something softer takes over. Not soft in the simpering, scented-lobby sense. Soft as in grounded. Leafy. Humane. The sort of softness that makes your shoulders drop half an inch before you have even reached the lifts. The kind that feels increasingly rare in hotels, and rarer still in city hotels, where “wellness” can sometimes mean a bowl of apples near reception and a treadmill facing a wall. At 1 Hotel Melbourne , wellness is not tucked away as an afterthought. It is in the DNA of the place. Which feels timely, because wellness travel is no longer a niche for the already converted. The Global Wellness Institute says wellness tourism expenditure reached US$894 billion in 2024, while Australia recorded 14.65 million wellness trips in 2023, including 14.02 million secondary wellness trips, meaning travellers who may not book a trip solely for wellness but still expect to sleep better, eat better, move better and feel more restored while they’re away. That was the thread running through the recent TravMedia wellness discussion too. People do not want a holiday after the holiday anymore. They want the trip itself to do some of the repair. And this hotel gets that. Checking in, I noticed the staff first. Everyone looked so implausibly fresh and healthy I briefly wondered whether they had all emerged from a breathwork session together. The uniforms, in deep green and navy, were cool without trying too hard. The welcome felt warm, efficient and oddly calming, which is not always the case at new luxury hotels, where you can sometimes sense the machinery whirring behind the smile. Then the details began to reveal themselves. Design, Sustainability and Biophilic Living A dramatic stone wall in the lobby. Vegetation climbing and spilling. Timber everywhere, but not in the polished, generic sense. This is timber with memory. Across the project, more than 2,000 original elements were salvaged and reincorporated, from pavers and trusses to doors and frames. There are more than 4,500 square metres of reclaimed timber throughout the hotel and over 7,000 plants bringing Victoria’s biodiversity indoors. It sounds like a lot on paper. In person, it simply feels alive. There are reclaimed elm trees from Melbourne’s Metro Tunnel works in the reception desk. Decommissioned railway bridge elements turned into a staircase. Timber panels marked by marine worms, salvaged from submerged piers, now repurposed into room details. The result could have felt too earnest, too designed, too desperate to prove its sustainability credentials. Instead, it feels warm, layered and deeply considered. That is one of 1 Hotel Melbourne’s greatest strengths. It feels less like a hotel and more like the very chic, very environmentally literate apartment of someone who owns linen sofas, sculptural dining chairs and extremely good taste in throws. There are little zones to perch in, to read in, to work in,…

articles.title: Kate Waterhouse on the Joy of Dressing Up
articles.author: Zoe Briggs
articles.excerpt: Kate Waterhouse on style, skin and stepping into her new role as Beauticate’s Style Editor
articles.body: Content creator, author and media personality Kate Waterhouse has long been a fixture in Australia's fashion landscape. Known for her polished yet approachable style, she has built a career spanning fashion commentary, television, brand partnerships and writing, including her popular Sophia and Gracie children's book series. For me, this one is personal. Kate and I have moved in the same circles for years, and Kate was one of the very first people we ever interviewed on Beauticate - more than twelve years ago. Back then, Kate welcomed us into her home – an apartment just down the road from this beautiful home – and we created some beauty videos together (flashback to How to do A Smokey Eye and How She Prepped Her Skin – we haven’t aged a bit – ha ha!) So when the time came to bring a Style Editor into the Beauticate fold, there was really only one person. Now, Kate brings that same generosity and considered eye to Beauticate in an official capacity: sharing her take on modern style, wardrobe staples and the pieces that truly work in real life. We visited her at her beautiful beachside home in Sydney, where she lives with her husband, two daughters and their much-loved Cobberdog. The space feels like an extension of her personal style. Thoughtful, elegant and quietly luxurious, yet warm and completely liveable. The kind of home that looks considered, but never overdone. Early Influences and the Racing World "So much of who I am and the shape that my life and career have taken has been informed by the glamour of the racing world. I grew up watching my mum get ready for the races; it was like magic to me. Saturdays were my ‘dress-up days’ – as she’d get ready, I’d be beside her trying on her clothes and raiding her accessories. Of course, then she left for the track and I’d have to clean up my mess! Beyond the glamour she introduced me to, what always stayed with me was her incredible work ethic. My mum is one of the hardest-working people I know. Watching her juggle so much with such determination inspires me to keep busy, embrace new projects and never shy away from: ‘wearing many hats’. Career, Creativity and Balance It’s been wonderful to be able to turn my passion into my profession. While studying Media and Communications at university, I began my career at The Sunday Telegraph, reporting on social pages and interviewing personalities. I was naturally drawn to fashion storytelling, which led me to become Style Editor before moving on to The Sun-Herald as Fashion Editor. During this time, I also wrote my “Date with Kate” column, where I had the opportunity to interview some of the world’s biggest names, from the Kardashians to Hailey Bieber and Sabrina Carpenter. I love experimenting with fashion and beauty – for me, that is self-expression and a creative outlet. I don’t feel an obligation to look a certain way. In my work I get to collaborate with some amazing brands and for those moments, I absolutely want to look polished. What you see online is only a fraction of the story, though. In reality there are just as many days when I’m in no-makeup-activewear-mode, answering emails and heading to school pick-up with messy hair. I see growing older as an honour. I actually feel more confident and comfortable in myself now than ever before. With age has come perspective, and that’s something I really value. When it comes to balancing my career and my home life, family will always come first. I…

articles.title: I Got Breast Cancer for Christmas
articles.author: Colette Harvey
articles.excerpt: A deeply personal account of breast cancer at 43 – from diagnosis to surgery, and the beauty rituals and essentials that helped along the way.
articles.body: Breast cancer now affects one in seven Australian women, and a diagnosis changes everything overnight. I never imagined one of those women would be one of my closest friends. Colette and I met when we were 18, working on our very first magazine together. She went on to become a respected publicist and magazine stylist. We’ve grown up side by side ever since. Careers, love, life, motherhood. So when she called to tell me she had breast cancer, the shock was immediate. And then, almost just as quickly, came something else. “I want to share this. If it helps even one woman.” For someone who has built a career behind the scenes, choosing to tell this story publicly is no small thing. What followed was not just her diagnosis, but the quiet, relentless work of figuring out how to navigate it. The things no one really prepares you for. Suddenly, you’re deep in Google searching cancer beauty tips, mastectomy recovery advice and what to actually pack in a hospital bag. It becomes a full-time job. And yet, so few women talk about what genuinely helps. The beauty rituals that make you feel like yourself again. The skincare that holds up during chemotherapy. The eyebrow treatments that frame your face when everything else feels unfamiliar. The hospital bag essentials that bring comfort when nothing else does. In this heartfelt piece, Colette shares her honest account of being diagnosed with breast cancer at 43, the products and treatments that carried her through, and the raw truths no one tells you. It’s the first in a series she’s bravely chosen to share. Breast cancer can impact every part of life, including identity and self-image. This story shares one woman’s experience navigating diagnosis, treatment and the small rituals that helped her feel like herself again. Sigourney x A Diagnosis That Changes Everything Breast cancer beauty tips are not something you expect to search for. My name is Colette. I’m 43 years old. I grew up and worked in Sydney’s East, spending more than two decades in media and fashion before moving to the Central Coast with my husband Joe, our little boy River, and three dogs. And well… I have always had great hair. No – I have always had fabulous hair. So fabulous that hairdressers used to fight over giving me blow-dries. Since my twenties, my hair quickly became my thing. Thanks to a string of incredible hairdressers – hello Reece and Kate from team Joh Bailey – I would leave the salon with a spring in my step and curls halfway down my back. What do they say? The bigger the hair, the smaller the problems. The Moment You Know A few weeks into November 2025, I was on my exercise bike at home when I felt a pain in my chest – my right breast to be exact. In that moment, I had a sinking feeling deep in my stomach. Back in July, we had gone to Bali for what was meant to be a month of utter bliss before I contracted Dengue fever and spent the entire holiday incredibly sick. So sick that I remember saying to my husband, “If I die, please make sure River remembers me… and no, you aren’t allowed to marry again.” True story. I had high fevers, hallucinations, every bone felt broken, and to top it off I was covered in a painful red rash. Just before I came down with the fever, sitting at dinner, I remember telling Joe I had felt a lump and made a mental note to get it checked when…

articles.title: Trinny Woodall on Reinvention, Resilience and Backing Yourself
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Trinny Woodall on reinvention, resilience and backing yourself – a powerful conversation on leadership, grief and showing up fully.
articles.body: In this Trinny Woodall podcast, I’m joined by the founder of Trinny London - one of the most refreshingly honest voices in beauty and business. But what makes Trinny so compelling isn’t just what she’s built. It’s how she’s rebuilt herself, again and again. In this Trinny Woodall podcast, I'm joined by the founder of Trinny London -- one of the most refreshingly honest voices in beauty and business. But what makes Trinny so compelling isn't just what she's built. It's how she's rebuilt herself, again and again. Trinny Woodall on reinvention, resilience and backing yourself – a powerful conversation on leadership, grief and showing up fully. Stop shrinking From addiction and grief to solo motherhood, leadership and reinvention, her story is one of depth, resilience and hard-won self-awareness. In this episode, we talk about what it really takes to keep showing up when life has stretched you, humbled you, or broken your heart a little. Trinny shares why she rejects the idea of imposter syndrome, how she’s learned to walk into rooms she once felt unqualified for, and why women need to stop shrinking themselves in spaces that were never designed for them. We also explore female friendship, social media, people-pleasing, leadership, and the subtle but powerful choice to either lift each other up or get caught in the noise. It’s a conversation about emotional maturity, courage, and learning how to be fully yourself – both in public and in private. Women need to stop shrinking themselves in spaces that were never designed for them. Along the way, Trinny shares the rituals that keep her feeling strong and steady – from meditation and weight training to SPF , ice facials and the small daily disciplines that help her return to herself. articles.title: Alexa Roetger on Skin, Self-Worth and Starting Over
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: This week I am joined by Alexa Roetger, founder of Aestheticá Byron Bay, for a conversation that goes beyond skin deep, into self-worth, motherhood and starting over.
articles.body: Listen to the full episode here This week I am joined by Alexa Roetger, founder of Aestheticá Byron Bay, for a conversation that goes beyond skin deep. Better known to many as Nurse Lex, she is a registered nurse, a skin expert, and one of those rare women whose work is deeply grounded in both science and soul. Publicly she has built a respected Byron Bay clinic known for its holistic, less-is-more approach to skin. Privately her story is one of resilience, reinvention, grief, motherhood, and learning to trust her own philosophy in an industry obsessed with trends. From Clinical Nursing to Aesthetic Medicine In this conversation Lex shares how she went from working in high-pressure clinical nursing to creating a business that helps women feel more at home in themselves. Not more perfect, just more aligned. We talk about the emotional side of aesthetics, the moment your reflection no longer feels like you, and why so many women are not really chasing youth at all, but recognition. Building a Business While Becoming a Mother We also go deeper into the realities of building a clinic while becoming a mother, including the surprise motherhood story that unfolded while she was growing Aestheticá. Lex is honest about the quiet power of word of mouth, and the grief that can reshape how you see women's health, hormones, ageing and care. It is a conversation about skin, yes, but also about identity, intuition, and what it means to support women honestly. Skin Health Before Trends Lex believes skin health should always come before trends. We talk through her thinking on barrier repair, regenerative treatments and respecting the skin, rather than chasing whatever is loudest online that season. She is clear that the best practitioners are not always the most visible. For her, growing a trusted business has come from integrity and reputation, built one patient at a time. Perimenopause and Not Recognising Yourself Some of the most moving parts of this episode sit with perimenopause and menopause, and the disorienting experience of not recognising yourself in the mirror. Lex speaks to how hormonal shifts affect the skin, and why this phase of life deserves honest, supportive care rather than generic anti-ageing advice. Nurse Lex on Life In this episode, we explore: - Lex's path from nursing into aesthetic medicine - The surprise motherhood story that unfolded while she was building her clinic - Why she believes skin health should come before trends - Her thoughts on barrier repair, regenerative treatments and respecting the skin - The emotional impact of perimenopause, menopause and not recognising yourself in the mirror - Why the best practitioners aren't always the loudest online - What it takes to grow a trusted business through integrity and reputation You will come away with a deeper understanding of skin, but also a deeper compassion for yourself, especially if you have ever felt like your outer self stopped matching the person you know you still are inside. If you loved this episode, I would be so grateful if you left a review on Apple Podcasts or Spotify. It helps us reach more women who need these conversations. articles.title: Susan Yara on Reinvention and Rebuilding Trust
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Beauty creator and Naturium founder Susan Yara joins me for an honest conversation about reinvention, online backlash, boundaries and the six rituals that keep her grounded.
articles.body: Susan Yara, beauty pioneer, entrepreneur and wellness advocate, joins me for a deeply honest conversation about reinvention, resilience and what it really means to be beautiful inside. Listen to the full episode here Some people build a following. Susan Yara built trust. The beauty content creator behind Mixed Makeup and founder of the skincare brand Naturium joins me for a deeply honest conversation about reinvention, resilience and what it really means to be beautiful inside. In this episode we go beyond the highlight reel, into the moments that shaped her and the ones that nearly broke her. From Outsider to Trusted Voice Susan shares her journey from feeling like an outsider as a child to building trust with millions of women. That early sense of not quite belonging never fully left her, but it became the thing that taught her to listen, to question and to speak plainly. It is also what made her so good at her work. The trust she built was never about being the loudest voice in beauty. It was about being a reliable one. The Hidden Cost of Online Criticism We talk openly about the psychological toll of online backlash, and how public scrutiny lands differently when your name is the brand. Susan is candid about the moments that hurt, and about how she learned to separate genuine feedback from noise. Out of that came a quiet discipline around boundaries. Setting them, she says, is not about shutting people out. It is about protecting the energy you need to keep showing up. When Wellness Stopped Being Optional There was a moment Susan realised wellness was not a nice-to-have, it was essential. We dig into self-care in the digital age, the pressure of perfection, and her approach to hormonal health. She is refreshingly practical about it. Rest, movement and looking after her body are not indulgences she earns. They are the foundation that lets everything else stand. Why a Trusted Inner Circle Matters One of the most powerful forms of protection, Susan says, is a small and trusted inner circle. When the outside world feels loud and quick to judge, the people who know the real you become a kind of anchor. She also opens up about motherhood and identity, and the ongoing work of holding on to herself while living a life that plays out in public. The Six Rituals That Keep Her Grounded When she needs to feel grounded, clear and herself again, Susan returns to six rituals. They are simple, repeatable and deeply personal, the small practices that bring her back to centre when everything else is in flux. It is a thoughtful, deeply human conversation about resilience, self-trust and choosing depth over noise. If you have ever felt the pull to keep performing, this one is a reminder that you are allowed to step back and rebuild. articles.title: Real Results: Beauticate Readers Trial Système Bio+ Oil Serum
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Beauticate readers trialled the Système Bio+ Oil Serum and documented real results across glow, hydration, fine lines and skin tone.
articles.body: We asked Beauticate readers to trial the Système Bio+ Oil Serum over two weeks, sharing before-and-after images and honest feedback. See the difference in glow, hydration and skin tone. TL;DR: Is the Systeme Bio+ Oil Serum worth it? Yes. Four Beauticate readers trialled it over two weeks and every one reported real results – improved hydration, visible glow and softer fine lines within days. The lightweight dry-oil formula works morning and night, under makeup, and across different skin types including sensitive skin. 3c96efce (Fix markdown delimiters in 30 articles (batch 2)) We were looking for real people with real skin concerns – dryness, dullness, fine lines, and loss of radiance – willing to document their experience honestly. Our readers were selected across different skin types and lifestyles, each committing to the trial. No scripts. No paid endorsements. Just the serum – and the results. What Is the Système Bio+ Oil Serum? What Does the Système Bio+ Oil Serum Contain? Système Bio+ Oil Serum is a French-formulated facial oil built around an active ingredient – ANTILEUKINE 6™ , derived from golden seaweed and clinically proven to hydrate, soothe and protect the skin. The formula also contains stable Vitamin C – rare in an oil format – along with Vitamin E, making it a true multi-tasker. And it is fragrance-free. The Bio+ Oil Serum is designed to target - Dehydration and dryness - Dullness and lack of radiance - Fine lines related to dehydration - Loss of suppleness in the face, neck and decolletage - Environmental skin stress What sets it apart is the texture. articles.title: Dr Shefali Tsabary: The Truth About Conscious Parenting, Screens and Shame
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Dr Shefali on conscious parenting, shame and burnout – a powerful conversation on boundaries, screens and coming back to yourself.
articles.body: This week on Beautiful Inside, I’m joined by Dr Shefali Tsabary - clinical psychologist, bestselling author, and the voice behind the Conscious Parenting movement. But what makes her story matter isn’t just her expertise. It’s the way she names the patterns so many of us are living inside: perfectionism dressed up as “good parenting”, approval-seeking disguised as “being a nice person”, and the silent burnout of holding everything together. In this conversation, you’ll feel both seen and steadied. Dr Shefali doesn’t offer fluffy fixes – she offers a mirror. One that helps you understand why you react the way you do, how to repair without drowning in shame, and what it actually looks like to come home to yourself in midlife. We talk about the emotional moments that make parenting (and womanhood) so charged: the outbursts that leave you rattled, the guilt that follows, and the fear that you’re “doing damage”. Dr Shefali shares a powerful reframe – that parenting isn’t a performance to perfect, but a relationship to grow through – and the relief in that lands in your body. Parenting isn’t a performance to perfect, but a relationship to grow through. Navigating the daily We also go deep on something many families are navigating daily: screens and tech dependence . Dr Shefali is clear-eyed about how dopamine, swiping, and constant stimulation are shaping our children (and us), and what it takes to set boundaries that don’t come from control, but from protection and leadership. And then, the conversation widens beautifully. Dr Shefali opens up about her own reinvention. Leaving India at 21, building a life in the US, and later shedding the identity of the “good wife” and the woman who performs stability. It’s raw, brave, and deeply liberating, especially for anyone standing at the edge of a life shift and wondering who they’ll be without the roles. In this episode - How to pause, reflect, and repair after you lose your temper. Without spiralling into self-hatred. - Why shame keeps women stuck, and how to start loosening its grip - The difference between life-enhancing boundaries and ego-enhancing boundaries (and why that matters at home) - What screen addiction is really doing to attention, connection, and family dynamics - The real root of burnout for so many women: the hunger for approval, validation, and praise - Dr Shefali’s beauty and wellness rituals - not as “self-improvement”, but as self-connection Thank you If this episode gave you language for what you’ve been feeling – or a gentle jolt of permission to change – I’d love you to leave a review on Spotify or Apple Podcasts. It helps more women find these conversations, and it tells the algorithm this is worth sharing.

articles.title: Trinny Woodall on Purpose and Picking Yourself Back Up
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Trinny Woodall on backing yourself: why she calls imposter syndrome a word invented by a man, how she chooses kindness over drama, and the hard years she would not give back.
articles.body: In this Trinny Woodall podcast, I’m joined by the founder of Trinny London - one of the most refreshingly honest voices in beauty and business. But what makes Trinny so compelling isn’t just what she’s built. It’s how she’s rebuilt herself, again and again. Listen to the full episode here Trinny Woodall starts a lot of mornings with her head in a basin of ice. Not for wellness theatre, but because, in her words, she wakes up and her face looks like a crumpled bed of nettles and she needs her brain to switch on. It is exactly the kind of detail that makes her so easy to love. Glamorous and entirely without pretence, in the same breath. You might know Trinny Woodall as the co-host of What Not To Wear , or as the founder of Trinny London, the beauty brand now worth hundreds of millions. But what she has really mastered is something quieter and harder to buy. She knows how to back herself. She was the very first guest I recorded for Beautiful Inside, and two years on she came back to talk about what business, reinvention and a few brutal years have taught her. A Word Invented By a Man Trinny has no time for imposter syndrome. None. "I hate the word imposter syndrome. I feel it was a word invented by a man." Her reframe is the most useful thing I have heard on the subject. If you walk into a room and feel you do not belong, she says, it is almost always because you do not yet have the knowledge everyone else is using. So go and get it. She still does it herself. In an intense financial meeting she will quietly type an unfamiliar acronym into her phone rather than nod along and pretend. The question she asks is simple: what do I need to learn so I can come back in the room and have a voice. That is the whole trick. Not confidence as a personality trait, but curiosity as a practice. She is just as deliberate about how she walks in. She wants to enter the room as a person, she says, not as a woman fundraising in a world where only two per cent of capital goes to women. Lift Each Other Up, or Step Away The theme Trinny keeps returning to is kindness, and its opposite, drama. Women, she says, can choose to lift each other up or pull each other down. It goes back to boarding school. At twelve or thirteen, desperate to be included, she traded gossip for belonging, until the day it hurt someone and stopped her cold. She has lived by a quiet rule ever since, and passed it to her daughter Lyla on her own way to boarding school. Whenever you feel it, step away from the drama. She gravitates towards the people who never need it. The cousin who only ever had a good word for anyone. The friends who pull you up rather than down. She keeps very different friendship groups on purpose, so she is never caught inside any one cycle. The Years She Would Not Give Back Trinny got clean from addiction in her twenties, after two stints in rehab and years of daily meetings. She has spoken often about losing Lyla's father. None of it is performed for sympathy. It is simply the material her resilience is made from. "I don't regret my years when I had a tough time because it's made me what I am today." The pain fades, she says, the way it does…

articles.title: Sun Safety, but Make it Chic
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A practical guide to chic sunscreens and stylish sun hats that make daily sun protection easier for adults and kids.
articles.body: A practical guide to chic sunscreens and sun hats - tested poolside, mid-negotiation, with a child who actively dodges SPF. Teaching sun safety is one of those parenting ideals that sounds serene in theory and plays out very differently in real life. In my case, it involves Lulu clocking my intentions from across the pool, physically recoiling the moment sunscreen appears, and me becoming extremely selective about what I'm willing to fight over. Which is why this guide exists. These are the sunscreens I trust, the ones I'll happily use on myself, and the ones Lulu will tolerate. Plus the hats that make sun protection feel chic rather than punitive. Because if it looks good, it's far more likely to happen. Why Sun Protection Still Matters (No Debate Required) There's been a lively debate in Australia lately about sunscreen, sparked by recalls and concerns around incorrect SPF labelling. I'm not here to wade into that – except to say this: we know the sun is damaging and dangerous, and it causes skin cancer, so we need to be protecting our skin. Period. The real risk with all this noise is that it turns people off sunscreen altogether. In a country with some of the highest rates of skin cancer in the world – where two out of three Australians will be diagnosed in their lifetime – that's alarming. Add talk of illegal sun beds resurfacing and teens potentially swinging back towards risky behaviours, and it's clear: Sun safety isn't optional. Some protection is always better than none. No resistance here. - Rationale 3 The Brilliance Tinted Serum SPF50+ This illuminating daily serum with SPF50+ imparts a more even tone with a glowing, transparent finish, while also safeguarding skin with their Zinc Fusion Technology. This is your skin, but better. - SkinCeuticals Ultra Facial Defense SPF50 A dermatologist-backed daily shield that blends seamlessly and sits perfectly under makeup. Easy textures, modern formulas and the kind of branding that helps sell the concept to reluctant users. - Naked Sundays SPF50+ Glow Crème The Australian SPF brand that made sunscreen genuinely covetable. Their Glow Crème doubles as a primer with a luminous, dewy finish — the kind of SPF you actually look forward to applying. Healthy, protected skin is the foundation of everything – which is why treatments like Sigourney's Qure Micro-Infusion trial have also been part of the conversation lately. Because if it looks good, it's far more likely to happen. Physical (Mineral) Sunscreens: The Necessary Compromise For kids – and for long, exposed pool days – physical sunscreens still matter. But let's be honest: a white cast is often part of the deal. The ones I reach for most often: - Mother SPF Clean, mineral protection that feels thoughtful and gentle – the kind you're comfortable putting on kids without hesitation. - Mukti Organics Organic, calm and skin-friendly. A reassuring choice when sensitive skin is part of the equation. - Go To Skincare The zinc sunscreen that manages to feel modern and wearable – which is no small achievement for mineral SPF. - Fuca A lighter, easier-to-spread mineral sunscreen that doesn't fight you quite as much as most zinc formulas. - Simka Sheer Mineral Milk Fluid and…

articles.title: Can Red Light Therapy Help Hair Thinning? What the Data (and Real Life) Suggests
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Hair thinning is deeply personal. We explore whether red light therapy can help, what the data shows, and why realistic expectations matter.
articles.body: Hair loss is deeply personal. And for many of us, it doesn’t happen just once. Sigourney shares her (and her husband Damien's) experience with thinning hair and unpacks whether red light therapy can help, what the data shows, and why realistic expectations matter. I first experienced it after my babies were born – that slow, confronting postpartum shedding that turns every shower into a small emotional reckoning. Then again during periods of intense stress, when lifting clumps of hair from the drain felt genuinely soul-destroying. I tried everything: shampoos, sprays, supplements, scalp massages, even prayer. If you've been there, you know it's not vanity. It's grief. Hair carries identity, health and confidence. Watching it thin can feel quietly devastating. My husband Damien's experience has been different, but just as familiar. His hair has been gradually thinning for years. Nothing dramatic. Just that slow, creeping change many men notice and rarely talk about. That uncertainty is what makes hair loss so unsettling. You don't wake up bald. You just wake up one day more aware. Why Hair Loss Rarely Has One Clear Cause Hair thinning can be driven by hormones, genetics, stress, inflammation, postpartum shifts, perimenopause, or simple ageing. Often, it's a mix of all of the above – which is why single-solution answers rarely feel satisfying. Most people searching for hair loss solutions are looking for the same thing: something that helps, something consistent, and something that doesn't come with dramatic side effects or unrealistic promises. Why We Decided to Try Red Light Therapy for Hair Thinning The Qure Skincare Q-Renew LLLT Helmet landed on my radar at a time when red light therapy had already become part of our household routine. I already know and trust Qure as a brand – we've previously explored their LED technology across skincare and at-home treatments, including their LED Face Mask and Neck & Décolletage system. So instead of filing this under interesting but unnecessary , we had a proper conversation about whether it was worth testing in real life. I didn't need it urgently – though who doesn't want thicker hair? Damien, on the other hand, felt like the perfect guinea pig. That felt honest. So rather than chasing miracle cures or overhauling routines, we decided to add one variable and observe what happened. Calmly. Transparently. With realistic expectations. Why Red Light Therapy Entered the Hair Conversation Red light therapy has quietly become part of modern wellness routines. It now shows up in skincare, recovery tools and longevity-focused tech – a shift we've explored recently through wearable health devices and nervous system regulation. Its move to the scalp feels less like a gimmick and more like a natural extension of that thinking. Hair follicles are metabolically active. They're sensitive to inflammation, circulation and hormonal signals. If light-based therapies can support skin and muscle recovery, it's reasonable to ask whether they may also support scalp health. But curiosity alone wasn't enough. The data had to stack up. What the User Study Actually Looked At The data behind Qure's helmet comes from a 16-week clinical user study, where men and women with mild to moderate pattern hair thinning used the helmet at home. Hair was measured at baseline and again after consistent use, using clinical imaging tools including trichoscopy and phototrichogram analysis. No adverse events were reported. It's important to be clear about one thing upfront: this wasn't a placebo-controlled trial. There was no sham helmet. Which means we can't claim definitive cause and effect. But it was a real-world, at-home study using objective measurement tools – and the outcomes were specific enough to…

And someone, usually your partner, becomes the unofficial pool cleaner. In our case, that someone was Damien, who spent hours each week fishing leaves out of the water thanks to a beautiful but wildly uncooperative gum tree towering over our yard. When we finally launched our robotic pool cleaner, he joked that I was “losing Jorge”, his imaginary, full-time pool-cleaning alter ego. (Shame. He was a bit cute. The Robotic Pool Cleaner That Actually Does What It Says (A proper road test of the Aiper Scuba X1) I’ve tested enough “smart” home tech to be deeply sceptical. So when the Aiper Scuba X1 arrived, I had one question: will this actually save us time, or just add another thing to manage? I can say this now with confidence: it has completely changed how we live with our pool. The Scuba X1 is cordless, powerful, and genuinely intelligent. It doesn’t just skim the obvious leaves – it cleans everything you don’t see too. Fine sand. Algae. Dust. Hair. Insects. All the micro-debris that standard filters quietly ignore. What surprised me most wasn’t the suction (which is enormous), but the MicroMesh™ ultra-fine filter . articles.title: The Lazy Girl's Guide to Summer Entertaining
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A relaxed, design-led guide to summer entertaining – from grazing boards to table styling shortcuts that look effortless, even when they're not.
articles.body: Summer arrived the way it always does in my life: loudly, socially, and with far too many opinions about table styling. It kicked off with my 44th birthday: a Mediterranean-themed pool party involving olive trees, sage green everything, too much rosé, and the realisation that entertaining is now my entire personality. Since installing a pool (and promptly running out of money), life has become entirely about hosting. Casual swims turn into grazing boards. “Just popping over” becomes a four-hour affair. And because I’m equal parts busy, lazy and deeply committed to things looking nice, I’ve developed a series of entertaining hacks that I’m more than happy to share. At this point in summer, the diary is a revolving door of different groups coming through, and I’m officially in repeat-host mode. These are the ideas, shortcuts and small details that make summer entertaining look effortless – even when it very much isn’t. Grazing Boards, But Make Them Strategic (What Yaz taught me, and what Pinterest confirmed) My friend Yaz did the grazing board for my birthday, and I watched her work like it was a masterclass. A few lessons worth sharing: How many cheeses do you actually need? - Three cheeses = intimate dinner - Four to five cheeses = proper party Always include - One soft (brie, camembert) - One hard (aged cheddar, manchego) - One wildcard (blue, truffle, whipped feta) Garnishes people forget (but always eat) - Honeycomb or hot honey - Pickled grapes - Roasted figs - Marinated olives with citrus peel - Fresh herbs (thyme, rosemary, basil flowers) - Micro Greens - Chilli and Lime Salt Pinterest tricks that are worth stealing - Cold meat roses (fold in half and roll it or use a shot glass – it works) Check out the video below! - Layered crackers in little piles (not flat, height matters) - Citrus slices or dried fruit tucked between cheeses for colour and scent - Sprinkle nuts or chocolate covered nuts/broken bits of chocolate throughout If you’re in full hosting mode, you’ll also love our latest on smart, low-effort upgrades in Ingredient-Smart Beauty Swaps . The New Spritz Era (Aperol, but she’s evolved) We’re officially in our spritz renaissance, and Aperol is no longer the only invite. What we served - Limoncello Spritz (with Symphonia Sparkling : so elite! Especially when my friend Vanda dressed to match) - Rosé Spritz ( Symphonia Rosé , endlessly chic) - A few special bottles of champagne for dramatic entrances The Linen Tablecloth Hack That Makes You Look Like You Have Your Life Together This is my number one hostess trick, and it has saved me more times than I can count. Before guests arrive - Throw your linen tablecloth in the washing machine on a quick rinse - Pop it in the dryer until it’s 70–80% dry - Pull it out slightly damp and lay it straight onto the table No ironing. No creases. No rage. The weight of the linen does the rest, and by the time people sit down it’s perfectly smooth, like you planned it this way all along. Hostess energy: calm. Unflustered. Slightly smug. If you want the same energy for your own night routine, revisit Home Alone, But Never Boring: My Nightly Beauty Routine . The Table Setting Formula I Use Every Single Time (Layering, colour and a little personality go a long way) My table-setting philosophy is simple: start with linen, layer with intention, then have a bit of fun. For Christmas, I asked for a sage green tablecloth from Bed Threads – partly because the colour fit my grey-green…

articles.title: Sacred Six on Escape, Intention and the Spas That Shape Us
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: I recorded this solo episode from Alba on the Mornington Peninsula, the spa that took me straight back to my twenties. This is the story of why Sacred Six exists, and how the right space can change the way you feel.
articles.body: Listen to the full episode here I am recording this from a daybed at Alba on the Mornington Peninsula, and I have just walked out of the water. This is a solo episode about why Sacred Six exists at all. About escape, about intention, and about the spas that quietly shape the way we see ourselves. Why Alba Took Me Back I have just finished filming Sacred Six: Best Destination Spas in Australia, and Alba is where it began to make sense to me. The moment I stepped into those curved concrete rooms and sank into the geothermal water, I was back in my twenties, back in the thermal spas of Switzerland, realising very clearly that this was the world I wanted to write about. It is strange how a place can do that. You arrive carrying your whole life, and within an hour the water has loosened something. I felt it then. I felt it again here. Sacred Six Is Not Just a List Sacred Six was never meant to be a ranking. It is about the places that fuse architecture, design and wellness in a way that feels transportive. The kind of spaces where you step out of your everyday life and into something more intentional, more imaginative, more restorative. A great spa is a piece of design before it is anything else. The light, the materials, the way the water meets the stone. When it is done well, the building does half the healing for you. What Makes a Spa Truly Exceptional In this episode I talk about what lifts a spa from lovely to unforgettable. It is rarely the menu of treatments. It is the intention behind the space. The silence that is built in rather than asked for. The detail that tells you someone cared about how you would feel, not just how it would photograph. Australia deserves its own Sacred Six because we have these places now, and most people do not know they exist. I wanted to put them on the map. How Place Has Shaped My Work These experiences have shaped my work, my perspective and my relationship with beauty and wellbeing over time. They taught me that beauty is not only what you put on your skin. It is where you choose to stand still. If you are craving escape, dreaming of travel, or simply curious about how place can change the way you feel, this episode is for you. If you have a destination you think belongs on my list, I would love to hear it. Please rate, review and share the episode if it resonated. It helps more than you know. A Skin-Sloughing Exfoliant Swipe on this award-winning lotion any time your skin is feeling too oily or clogged up to prevent breakouts and brighten. 6. A Glow Serum Who doesn't want luminosity? This skincare-makeup hybrid delivers in spades and is a firm favourite among anyone chasing that lit-from-within finish. 7. A Drying Lotion I can't count the number of times this little pink lotion has saved my bacon. Often it dries pimples out overnight. 8. A Clay Mask For those days when a breakout is imminent, apply this detoxifying mask to problem areas to draw out oil and bacteria. 9. A Non-Oily Oil This somehow balances oily skin, quenches dry skin, and doubles as a beautiful primer for makeup. Go-To's products are en pointe . 10. A Cleansing Tool Tools take your cleansing to the next level and will help minimise blackheads and breakouts. --- Twenties Your twenties are about learning what your skin loves and protecting it before you ever think you need to. Daily sunscreen (yes, I know I harp on), thorough cleansing and antioxidants to protect and prevent premature ageing. 11. The 'Clean' Sunscreen Some people worry about chemicals in their sunscreen. This one is delightfully low-tox and still nice to wear. 12. The Lazy-Girl's Cleanser For those nights when you can barely be bothered to remove your makeup, keep this bottle and some reusable pads stashed on your night stand. 13. The Sun Protecting CC Cream Another cult product that delivers a flawless complexion with SPF 50+ and skincare properties. 14. The Cult Vitamin C I still use this daily and I notice when I don't. It truly does deliver bright, glowing skin in a bottle. You should use this at every age. 15. The Do-Everything Cream The ultimate makeup artist's moisturiser — it primes perfectly for foundation and can also be used as a masque or cleanser. 16. Cleansing Pads If you wear a lot of makeup these are a genius and sustainable way to remove it, along with sunscreen. 17. The Date Night Mask This deliciously peppermint-scented yellow concoction uses rosehip seeds, turmeric and papaya enzymes to brighten…

articles.title: 38° The Bathhouse, Bondi Beach
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A domed magnesium pool held at 38 degrees, ice baths, infrared suites and a mirrored ceiling that reads like the ocean at sunset. Sculptural, social and a little hypnotic.
articles.body: The room formerly known as Slow House reopened in late 2025 with a new name and a warmer heart. Under Bondi, beneath the Beachouse gym, is a warren of sandstone-toned rooms built around a single glowing domed magnesium pool held at 38 degrees, which is where the name comes from. GIANT Design gave it soft organic curves and a mirrored ceiling that reads like the ocean at sunset. Around it sit more magnesium plunges at varying temperatures, two roomy ice baths, a Finnish sauna, a steam room and four private infrared suites. Come Monday mornings there is a free sound session. Sculptural, social and a little hypnotic. Come for the circuit, stay for the quiet.

articles.title: Aalto Community, Goodwood
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A no-membership Finnish sauna and ice bath studio on King William Road, surrounded by roughly 150 plants and built on the idea of accessibility.
articles.body: Roughly 150 plants share the room with one large Finnish sauna and three ice baths. That is the whole pitch, and it works. Aalto Community sits on King William Road in Goodwood, and it decided early that the point was not exclusivity. There is no membership. You drop in. Co-founder Tom Emmett keeps coming back to one word, accessibility, whether you are a local or someone's interstate visitor killing a spare afternoon. Warm up, plunge, sit in the foyer with a tea, do it again. The greenery softens everything. A bathhouse that would rather you felt welcome than initiated.

articles.title: Alchemy Saunas, East Fremantle
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A heritage pub turned Roman-inspired bathhouse. Alchemy Saunas fills the 120-year-old Royal George on Duke Street with a 50,000 litre ice pool, hot magnesium pool, three saunas and a steam room across two storeys.
articles.body: The Royal George has been a lot of things in 120 years. Horse stables. A hotel. A pub. A restaurant. Now the heritage building on Duke Street holds a 50,000 litre ice pool and a hot magnesium pool across two storeys, the most ambitious thing Alchemy has built. The brief was Roman bathhouse meets contemporary sauna. Two years of work went in before the doors opened in June. Memberships sold out before anyone had bathed. There are three saunas, a steam room and ice showers, and the old bones of the place hold all of it. Book a casual session. The locals already have.

articles.title: Capybara Bathing, Surry Hills
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: The most beautiful of Sydney's new bathhouses. Capybara turns a 1939 Surry Hills warehouse into a terracotta-tiled ritual of magnesium heat, cedar sauna and cold plunge.
articles.body: Six friends, four of them architects, took the ground floor of a 1939 warehouse on Commonwealth Street and made the most beautiful bathhouse of the new wave. They kept the old concrete beams and timber joists raw, then carved curved portals into the walls so the space reveals itself slowly, one zone at a time. There is a cedar sauna waterproofed in deep red, terracotta showering nooks with ceramic basins one of the co-founders threw himself, and a magnesium bath at a steady 38 degrees. The circuit is guided and communal, twenty people at most, moving from heat to a two-person ice plunge to a bench of crushed ice for scrubbing. Leif botanicals sit in the showers. The Local Project put it in print, and you will see why in the first thirty seconds. This is bathing as architecture. Nothing else in Sydney looks quite like it.

articles.title: CHANGE Wellness, North Adelaide
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A 36 degree magnesium pool, twin ice baths and a trio of heat on O'Connell Street. Sixty minutes, no set order, recovery staged like theatre.
articles.body: The lighting changes through the day. So does the music, shifting with the hours as if the room were paying attention to you. CHANGE Wellness opened on O'Connell Street with a 36 degree magnesium pool at its centre, twin ice baths on either side, and a trio of heat in a traditional sauna, an infrared sauna and a steam room. You get sixty minutes and no set order. Move between hot and cold at whatever pace your body asks for. There is a private suite if you would rather not share. Recovery, staged like theatre. You leave looser than you arrived.

articles.title: Cloud 9 Sauna, MacMasters Beach
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Two garden saunas on the Scenic Road at MacMasters Beach. One infrared, one Finnish. No spa lobby. No upsell. Just heat, garden and quiet.
articles.body: There are two of them, set apart in the garden, timber paths running between. One is the Bali Garden, an infrared room that holds a gentle fifty to sixty degrees and takes up to three. The other is the Zen Garden, a proper Finnish sauna that climbs to eighty, dry or steamed however you like it, and seats four. You choose your heat, then walk out into greenery to cool down between rounds. It is on the Scenic Road at MacMasters Beach, which is exactly the sort of address that suits it. No spa lobby. No upsell. Just heat, garden and quiet.

articles.title: Comma, Cremorne
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A six-person bathhouse in Cremorne designed by architect Eloise Fotheringham. Sauna, soak, sweat in Scandinavian order, with custom Ross Gardam lighting and monastic restraint.
articles.body: Six people. That is the entire capacity at Comma, and the restraint tells you everything about it. Architect Eloise Fotheringham built the Cremorne bathhouse around the idea that solitude is a practice rather than an indulgence, then pared the space back until only the essentials remained. Sauna, soak, sweat, in the Scandinavian order. The lighting is custom Ross Gardam, the Nebulae pendants throwing a soft glow over surfaces kept almost monastic. Robes and towels are laid out, phones are not welcome, and the whole thing runs on stillness. An inner-city bathhouse that behaves like a destination spa an hour from anywhere. Book it for one. That is how it was designed.

articles.title: else BATHHOUSE, South Melbourne
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A five-million-dollar restoration of an 1880s Emerald Hill building, stacking mineral pools, cold plunges and saunas beneath two open-air rooftop pools. Victorian bones, Nordic ritual.
articles.body: An 1880s building in the historic heart of Emerald Hill is not the obvious place for a bathhouse. else has made it one. Spread across three levels of a heritage shell, the raw brick and old timber left to speak for themselves, it stacks mineral pools, cold plunges and saunas beneath two open-air rooftop pools where you bathe with the South Melbourne sky overhead. There is an alpine cabin and a vitality pool. The bones are Victorian. The ritual is Nordic. A five-million-dollar restoration that took its heritage delays on the chin and kept the building intact. Sky bathing above a nineteenth-century street. Worth the wait.

articles.title: Floating Sauna Lake Derby, Derby
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Two floating sheds on a former tin mine, lined in burnt larch and shortlisted at the national architecture awards. Architecture you can sweat in.
articles.body: Two little sheds sit out on the water, one black, one white, gabled like something from a child's drawing. They float. Licht Architecture anchored them to a pontoon on Lake Derby and ran a footbridge out from the shore, and the result was shortlisted at the national architecture awards. The sauna inside is lined in dark burnt larch. The changing room glows, its screening turning occupants into soft silhouettes. Lake Derby is not natural. It filled a tin mine that closed decades ago, and now it cools mountain bikers who plunge straight off the deck between rounds of heat. Architecture you can sweat in. Then jump.

articles.title: MEND, Margaret River
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Contrast bathing stripped to its essentials. MEND in Margaret River pairs a Finnish sauna and infrared sauna with hot plunge and ice bath, all in cedar and neutral tones.
articles.body: MEND does the two things that matter and does them properly. There is a traditional Finnish sauna for dry heat and an infrared one for the slow burn, then a hot plunge and an ice bath to swing you between the extremes. Massage and bodywork sit alongside for the days you want hands involved. The design is pared back and earthy, what the founders call humble luxury, which in Margaret River reads as cedar, neutral tones and nothing shouting. It is the contrast bathing circuit stripped to its essentials. Hot. Cold. Repeat. Then a long drink of water and the drive home.

articles.title: Merse Wellness, Osborne Park
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Perth's largest magnesium pool, cold plunge pools, two saunas and a full recovery lounge with compression boots, LED therapy and sound healing on Scarborough Beach Road.
articles.body: Perth's largest magnesium pool is the headline here, and it earns it. Merse took over a stretch of Scarborough Beach Road in Osborne Park and filled it with warm mineral water, cold plunge pools and two kinds of sauna. The hot-rock room for the purists. The infrared for everyone easing in. Between rounds there are monsoon showers and a steam room, then the Rejuvenate Lounge, which is where the technology lives. Compression boots. LED in four colours. Massage guns and sound healing on a loop. It is a lot of recovery under one roof. You will leave loose. Come early. It fills.

articles.title: Nova Holistic Spa, Hobart
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Hobart's only boutique all-weather outdoor contrast experience. Infrared sauna, magnesium spa and ice bath cycled under open Tasmanian sky.
articles.body: Rain or shine, the bathing here happens outdoors, which in Hobart takes a certain commitment to the idea. Nova calls itself the city's only boutique all-weather outdoor contrast experience, and on Goulburn Street it delivers exactly that. An infrared sauna, a magnesium spa and an ice bath, cycled hot to cold under open Tasmanian sky. There is more to the place than the water. Naturopathy, skin therapies, holistic counselling, even a tarot reading if the mood takes you. But the bathhouse is the heart of it. Book it private, or share it. Cold air, hot water, the whole point of winter reversed.

articles.title: Onsen, Torrensville
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Japanese bathing ritual on Henley Beach Road. Traditional sauna at ninety-five degrees, warm and cold mineral baths, and compression therapy for legs that have earned it.
articles.body: The traditional sauna runs hot, ninety to ninety-five degrees, the kind of heat that empties your head in minutes. Onsen brought the Japanese bathing ritual to Henley Beach Road in Torrensville and built the whole experience around contrast. You move from the sauna to a warm mineral bath, then into a cold mineral plunge, and repeat until your nervous system gives up the fight. There is a private infrared room and compression therapy for legs that have earned it. Twenty-five minutes a station, no rushing. Adelaide has plenty of saunas now. This one asks you to slow down and mean it.

articles.title: Sol Saunas, Prahran
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A social sauna in Prahran clad in charcoal and pale blonde timber. Nordic palette, no phones, no performance. Heat shared the Scandinavian way.
articles.body: Sol was built on an idea the Scandinavians take for granted. That heat is better shared. The Prahran space runs on it, a social sauna clad in charcoal and pale blonde timber where strangers end up talking on the tiered benches and then plunging cold together afterwards. The palette is Nordic. Restrained, warm, unfussy. Sessions move between the sauna and the cold, the rhythm doing the work, the conversation doing the rest. No phones, no performance, just the oldest wellness ritual there is done properly. Connection to yourself and to the people beside you. That is the whole pitch. It holds.

articles.title: Tank Bathhouse & Champagne Bar, Mooloolaba
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Six botanical-infused hot tubs on the water at Mooloolaba with a champagne bar at arm's reach. Bathing as a day out, with magnesium soaks, dry sauna and Mediterranean degustation on site.
articles.body: Six hot tubs sit on the water at Mooloolaba, each infused with botanicals and set to a different temperature, and there is a champagne bar an arm's reach from the pool. That is the Tank pitch and it is a good one. This is the waterfront sibling, all magnesium soaks and dry sauna, with Riviera doing Mediterranean degustation on site. You can even take a champagne cruise along the water afterwards if the mood holds. It is bathing as a day out rather than a solemn ritual, and there is nothing wrong with that. Bring a friend. Order the bubbles. Stay for the sunset over the marina.

articles.title: The Bathhouse Albion, Albion
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: The flagship of the Bathhouse Group, carved in travertine inside the Albion Fine Trades precinct. European-referenced bathing with Finnish saunas, vitality pools and a working fireplace.
articles.body: Ten spaces, all carved in travertine, sit inside the Albion Fine Trades precinct on Nariel Street. This is the flagship of the Bathhouse Group and the architects Hogg & Lamb have kept the European reference honest. Two vitality pools hold at 38 degrees. The cold plunge sits at 12. There is a Finnish sauna with a working fireplace, a second traditional sauna, two infrared rooms and a steam room tiered for sitting. You move through heat and cold in a loop, then settle in the tea lounge with something warm. Dyson and Sans in the change rooms is a nice touch. Come early. It fills.

articles.title: Vikasati Bathhouse, Southport
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Outdoor contrast therapy under open sky on the Gold Coast. Vikasati runs a 37-degree magnesium pool, cold plunge, ice baths and the Coast's largest traditional sauna from six in the morning.
articles.body: Vikasati does the whole thing outdoors. No walls, no roof over the pools, just Southport sky from six in the morning until the stars come out. The contrast therapy is the draw. A 37-degree magnesium pool, a 14-degree cold one, ice baths at five, and what they claim is the Gold Coast's largest traditional sauna. You move between hot and cold and let the temperature do the work. It is elemental and a little bracing and, at forty-nine dollars for ninety minutes, refreshingly unprecious about it. Wear your swimmers. Watch the light change over the ninety minutes. Nature is part of the process here, not the backdrop.

articles.title: Aesop, Paddington
articles.author: Jennah Porter
articles.excerpt: Aesop's Paddington outpost on Glenmore Road offers 60- and 75-minute customised facials from $240, inside a swimming pool-inspired interior by Clare Cousins Architects.
articles.body: Known for their minimalist formulas, fusion of plant-based and laboratory-made ingredients, as well as the stunningly designed shop floors, Aesop has always been a delight to shop for and to use. Although, deep in the basement of Aesop's flagship store in Paddington, there is a secret sanctuary for weary, dry or dull skin. As I descend into the Japanese-inspired treatment room, renowned facialist Sabrina Kafka-Girard greets me with a selection of calming herbal teas and tucks me into the luxurious white linen folds of the treatment table. I take a deep breath before disappearing into a state of Zen. The facial begins with a deep Parsley Seed Oil cleanse. Sabrina blends with raw ingredients, working with vitamins, antioxidants and plant extracts. She explains that these are mixed with the Aesop products so she can tailor the treatment to suit my individual skin type (quite dry, and often sensitised to some ingredients). Next, bases of green clay and fine white China clay are applied to draw impurities out of the skin before an indulgent lathering of moisture. The entire application is meticulous and Sabrina's training as a former masseuse transcends her subject into a state of tactile bliss. Meanwhile my sensitive skin happily absorbs the botanicals and I'm spoilt with applications of deliciously fragrant raw ingredients such as jasmine, chamomile and the rare Madagascan ylang ylang flower. Overall, it's a totally individualised experience that's set to become my new skincare ally. Perfect for anyone wanting to nourish their skin, while checking out of real life to instead spend a few fleeting hours of tranquil bliss. The entire 90-minute treatment leaves me feeling refreshed, but in a state of calm that lasts all day. Review by Jennah Porter

articles.title: Aesthetica, Byron Bay
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A calm, cruelty-free skin clinic in Byron Bay's Habitat precinct offering injectables, skin needling, LED, PRP and skin nutrition consults.
articles.body: Habitat is the industrial precinct where Byron keeps its good coffee and its architects. Aesthetica sits inside it, which tells you something before you walk in. The room is calm rather than clinical, run by medical and dermal people who clearly did not want it to feel like a hospital. The menu is proper. Injectables, skin needling, LED, PRP, plasma lift and a skin nutrition consult if you want to fix things from the inside. It is locally owned, cruelty-free and signed up to Sustainable Salons. Results without the sterile chill. That is a harder balance than it looks.

articles.title: Agape Hair, Hobart
articles.author: Beauticate Editorial
articles.excerpt: 1/148 Collins St, Hobart TAS 7000.

articles.title: All Saints Skin Clinic, Double Bay
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: A palatial Double Bay clinic by aesthetic physician Dr Joseph Hkeik, designed by Blainey North and devoted to the art of undetectable cosmetic work.
articles.body: Over ten years in the making, All Saints Skin Clinic in Double Bay is the creation of aesthetic physician to the A-list, Dr Joseph Hkeik. Situated in a designer-finished house that feels more like a palatial home than a clinic, the chic two-level space was imagined by Hkeik and brought to life by interior designer Blainey North. It features six treatment rooms, a skin consultation room complete with makeup and photography station, and even a meditation zone for clients to decompress post-treatment. With a client list that reads like a who's who of Australian celebrity, Hkeik is known for his holistic view of aesthetic treatments, and the concept behind his Double Bay clinic showcases that perfectly. His approach is one of restraint: creating work that is undetectable. "Maintaining normal facial expressiveness is fundamental in my eyes. I believe that less is more. This is at the heart of my 'art of face' philosophy. You will walk out of All Saints Skin Clinic feeling and looking more beautiful, natural and radiant," says Hkeik. The Double Bay clinic is the third All Saints practice, joining sister properties in Darlinghurst and Parramatta. Review by Sigourney Cantelo

articles.title: Amy Jean Brows, Sydney
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: St James Trust Building, Suite 1020/185 Elizabeth St, Sydney NSW 2000, 0447 167 227. Australia's original brow artist, now with five salons nationally and her own Privee Collection.
articles.body: Australia's Original Brow Artist Stepping into the exclusive Bambini Trust building, you know you're about to have a luxurious experience. And Amy Jean's diminutive salon doesn't disappoint. Regarded as the "Arch Angel" to Australia's A-List, AJ has built a reputation as being the best at her business, and that is the business of "dressing the eyes". Fresh Blooms and Bespoke Wallpaper Decorate the Space Just as a couturier creates bespoke garments for his clientele, Amy Jean analyses her clients' face and creates stunning lashes and brows that perfectly frame the eyes, which she has done for everyone from Dannii Minogue to Delta Goodrem. She currently has four salons in Sydney, Melbourne, the Gold Coast and Brisbane and is so in demand she has done pop-up salons in Perth and Paris. The Art of Dressing the Eyes "I believe eyes are windows to the soul," says Amy Jean passionately. "I love to create and I've always been a keen artist." Although it can take months to secure an appointment with the eye stylist herself, AJ has trained her staff in her particularly precise technique and she closely coaches them to maintain a top level of service. Inside the Chic Sydney Salon However it's Amy Jean's service I'm lucky enough to experience today. As I step into the chic dark-walled space of the reception, I take in the sparkling chandelier and a shiny gold plaque above the desk announcing "Amy Jean Eye Couture". There's soft lighting and a vase laden with fresh red roses. The waiting room is filled with the mouthwatering caramel scent emanating from Amy Jean's very own branded candle. There are fashion-focused coffee table books for me to flick through and a range of AJ's preferred products at eye height for play and purchase, including Dr Spiller skincare, Priori Lash Recovery Serum and her own range of Eye Couture products. I'm a big fan of the Eyebrow Putty and I can't resist stroking the silky soft makeup brushes that are on display. Above the register a top shelf is lined with bottles of Bollinger, a clue to Amy Jean's bubbly personality. AJ Is Known for Her Precision and Knack with Tweezers Amy Jean Palazzo Candles in Coconut Splice Fill the Room Brow Shaping and Lash Lift Experience I don't have to wait long as the brow queen herself sweeps in wearing a black bodycon dress and towering YSL Tribute heels. Her platinum hair frames an immaculately made up face with wide lash-lined eyes. There's no mistaking it, she's a walking advertisement for her business. We step into her white, light-filled treatment room where the walls are papered with pink flamingos and there are white roses spilling out of a vase in the corner. I settle back into the treatment bed, ready for my brow shape and lash lift (which involves perming the lash so it stands up by itself and tinting it, negating the need for mascara). AJ is also an expert in Feathertouch, a form of brow tattooing for sparse or patchy brows, sadly I can't try this as I'm pregnant, but I make a note to do it as soon as I'm able to. The Results: Defined Arches and Curled Lashes The next hour goes by in a flash as we gossip and catch up on life, before AJ presents me with a hand mirror to admire her handiwork. I'm stunned. My straggly brows have been replaced by sharp, defined arches and my lashes, which were looking stubby and sad after months of extension-abuse, are tinted and curled, which apparently lasts for eight weeks. Every service is…

articles.title: Bare Beauty House, Manly
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Eco-luxe hair, facials and nails in a heritage terrace on Pittwater Road. Bare Beauty House is the Northern Beaches one-stop shop for sustainable pampering.
articles.body: Eco-Luxe Hair and Beauty Salon This sustainable salon ticks so many boxes. Occupying a coveted corner position on Manly’s Pittwater Road is eco-luxe hair and beauty salon Bare Beauty House. Stretched over two levels of a converted heritage terrace, the salon is a true one stop shop offering expert colour, facials, massages and flawless nails using sustainable and cruelty-free products. Occupying a coveted corner position on Manly's Pittwater Road is eco-luxe hair and beauty salon Bare Beauty House. Stretched over two levels of a converted heritage terrace, the salon is a true one stop shop offering expert colour, facials, massages and flawless nails using sustainable and cruelty-free products. Inside it's all earthy tones from the raw brickwork, tan leather styling chairs and potted plants. The back mani/pedi room opens to a leafy courtyard that can play host to private bookings and pamper parties. Sustainable Products and Flawless Nails Since moving to the Northern Beaches in 2020, I've become quite the regular at Bare. Owner Naomi Browner looks after my cut and colour, and I love that I can multi-task beauty and hair. The Dazzle Dry manicures are some of the best I've had: the polish is hard wearing, almost as resilient as gels but much less damaging. Plus they're dry in five minutes, so you don't smudge anything when you're fishing out your keys. Salt Scrub and Massage Bliss Today I'm here for a colour touch up and cut and a scrub/massage which I've scheduled for myself as a little mid-winter treat. I head up the staircase into the hush of one of two sage-toned beauty rooms. The lights are low and the bed is cosy as my therapist Kana begins her work, scrubbing each limb with a deliciously scented salt scrub. The beauty treatments use either organic brand Eve Taylor (today I'm enjoying the scrub and oil) or Australian clean cosmeceutical Synergie, which I'm a huge fan of. I'm relieved to find that the scrub is quite dry (with just a touch of oil) so I don't get as cold as I usually do during body treatments. Deep Massage and Total Renewal I'm lulled nearly to sleep with Kana's rhythmic salty strokes and when she's finished, need to rouse myself to get up and have a shower. I marvel at my baby soft skin, deliciously coated with the oil, even after I step out of the shower. I settle back onto the bed for another hour of massage bliss, nodding off into a near-meditative state. Kana increases the pressure perfectly on my request and works out some stubborn knots in my neck and shoulder. I stumble down the stairs into daylight, happily submitting to my root touch up with Rebecca (Naomi JUST had a beautiful baby boy.) Organic Colour and Beautiful Blowdry The team uses Oway, which is a biodynamic organic hair range from Italy that performs as well as other professional colours but is gentle on my sensitive scalp. My greys covered and brassiness toned, and Frankie sets to work giving me a beautiful blowdry before finishing it off with a curling tong. A Northern Beaches Beauty Ritual And with that, it's back into the world, feeling totally renewed and reminded, yet again, of the importance of scheduling those little moments of self care for ourselves. If you can combine a little pampering with your usual beauty-maintenance, as you can at Bare Beauty House, then it's a no-brainer. Review by Sigourney Cantelo

articles.title: Bixie Colour, Caringbah
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
articles.excerpt: Clients fly interstate for Sheree Knobel's finesse balayage. Bixie Colour in Caringbah is the specialist colour salon with a cult Instagram following.
articles.body: Specialist Colour Salon in Caringbah Sitting politely on the Kingsway in Caringbah (a busy artery to Cronulla), Bixie Colour is a little haven of calm. The chic colour specialist salon is home to industry veteran Sheree Knobel, who is also the dab hand behind Jennifer Hawkin’s enviable shade of blonde. The Gorgeous Decor Makes You Feel Right at Home Sheree, who has spent the last 15 years working in the country’s best salons (she spent eight at Valonz), has also traveled the world, learning from the very best (including JLo’s and Emma Stone’s colourist Tracey Cunningham). And although she’s not currently taking on new clients, she imparts this knowledge passionately to her team of eight, which includes two senior full time colourists) and oversees many of the transformations which happen in her stylish salon. Arriving for a Colour Transformation When I make the journey south to Caringbah, I have high hopes. My colour is looking particularly fried and flat, and I swear my greys are multiplying by the day. This appointment can’t come soon enough. I find a park easily and enter the bright, buzzing salon. It’s a gorgeous space, all white with marble and rose gold accents. The whir of hairdryers and trill of girly chatter give it a relaxed, upbeat vibe. Sheree and I have a chat about my colour and she suggests going through the roots with a warm brown, then says she will do some “finesse balayage ” to create some lightness and variation through the ends. It’s finer and more precise than regular balayage . “This means you won’t get an obvious regrowth, which is great for you as you mentioned you find it hard to find the time to get to the salon. It gives you commitment-free lightness!” she announces triumphantly and starts painting on the colour. The Story Behind the Bixie Name Sheree opened the salon a mere five months ago. “I wanted a really nice space, a colour salon that is also family-focused, in that the staff could come to work in a nice environment,” says Sheree proudly. The name “Bixie” comes from the mythical creature by the same name, that changes its appearance multiple times. Perfect for the colour-savvy clientele that the salon attracts. Sheree says many of their customers travel from far-flung locations. The Successful Salon Opened Only Five Months Ago Bixie is Well Worth a Long Travel for Some Clients Clients Who Travel From Everywhere “Our clients travel from everywhere. I had a lady from Dubai yesterday, I have a whole crew of people that fly down Hamilton Island, and a lady that drives down from Dubbo,” she laughs, “I think they found us on Instagram… People are hair crazy. Instagram has helped with that. They know what good hair looks like.” As for her most famous client? “I’ve done Jen’s hair for 8 years. I was colouring her makeup artist, Liz Kelsh’s hair, and Jen used to always comment on her colour and say how gorgeous it was, but at the time I was on maternity leave. She ended up contacting me at home, and I would do her colour at home. I did her wedding colour with a five-day newborn baby in my lounge room, with the paparazzi waiting outside!” Beautiful Balayage Results Less than an hour later, I’m reclining in the black leather lounge blissing out to stylist Nasser’s insanely good head massage. He does an Olaplex treatment on me before giving me one of the best round-brush blowdries I’ve seen in a long time (look mum, no curling tong!). The colour looks beautiful, all caramel…

articles.title: Blanc, Perth
articles.author: Tess Schlink
articles.excerpt: Dr Clara Hurst brings Harley Street expertise to this exquisitely designed Cottesloe clinic, where bespoke facials and natural-looking injectables attract Perth's most discerning beauty devotees.
articles.body: A Discreet Cottesloe Cosmetic Clinic Situated in a tranquil corner of the well-heeled Perth suburb of Cottesloe is Blanc, a discreet cosmetic clinic offering natural-looking and bespoke treatments to the city’s most demanding beauty lovers. Tucked away from the glossy boutiques of Cottesloe’s main thoroughfare, Napoleon Street, the space is perfectly polished (it was designed by interior architect Sarah Coghlan from Within) and features chic furniture pieces from James Said and Mobilia in muted tones of pale grey and pink. Walls are adorned with ethereal paintings by local artist Francesca Gnagnarella, while the clinic’s floral displays are crafted by the very talented Natural Art Flowers. The clinic is scented with its own signature fragrance, blended by the nearby clean beauty destination, Heartwood. Dr Clara Hurst: Harley Street Expertise Behind the clinic is the glamorous Dr Clara Hurst, educated at the prestigious King’s College London Medical and Dental School, she worked as a cosmetic injector in Harley Street, London’s most sought-after address for all things medical, before heading to Australian shores and setting up shop. The Signature Facial Experience I arrive at Blanc to experience their Signature Facial some two weeks before my wedding for a much-needed complexion pep, the stress-induced insomnia having unfortunately taken a toll on the bridal radiance I was aiming for. My therapist, Gemma, ushers me into a peaceful treatment room with a blush-hued sink kitted out with Aesop handwashes, these subtle touches make for a chic and very welcoming space. Bespoke Treatments for Every Skin From the moment the facial begins, it’s evident that Blanc are serious about making their treatments truly bespoke to each client’s skincare needs, Gemma meticulously assesses my skin condition before selecting just the right cleansers to prep my skin and concocting the perfect peel for me. Throughout the many skin-beautifying steps in the treatment (facial steaming, electrical muscle stimulation and a 3D nano crystal mask) I enjoy a deep massage not only to my face and décolleté , but to my arms and legs as well. I spend a blissful 90 minutes slipping in and out of sleep while Gemma coaxes my skin into submission. At the end of the treatment, she places me under an LED light for some serious skin brightening, before applying a bespoke selection of products to maximise that coveted after facial glow. Injectables, Laser and Plasma Pen Beyond luxurious facials, Blanc provide a suite of beautifying treatments. Their cosmetic injectables are particularly sought-after, thanks to the clinic’s signature subtle and natural looking results. The clinic also provides a host of cutting-edge dermal therapies, with a range of rejuvenating laser and peel treatments on offer, as well as the skin-tightening Accor Plasma Pen (they are the only clinic in WA where the treatment is available), plus waxing and eyelash tinting to round out the beautification offerings. Hydrated and Illuminated Results I leave the clinic and my skin looks (and feels) much better than it has in a while. It’s hydrated and illuminated, cleverly masking the stress and insomnia of the preceding weeks. I am itching at the chance to return to Blanc to sample more of the treatments that have quickly made them a local beauty lovers’ go-to, but am content to savour my much-appreciated pre-wedding glow in the meantime.

articles.title: Brad Ngata Hair Direction, Darlinghurst
articles.author: Sigourney Cantelo
